base_rates.claim: With microcaps neutralized (NYSE breakpoints, value weights), 65% of 452 anomalies fail t > 1.96 and 82.1% fail a multiple-testing hurdle of t > 2.78; the trading-frictions category fails 96%. Surviving anomalies have much smaller economic magnitudes than originally reported.
base_rates.number: 65% fail t>1.96; 82% fail t>2.78; 96% of friction anomalies fail
base_rates.source: Hou, Xue & Zhang, Review of Financial Studies 2020, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3275496
base_rates.applicability: Direct for the overflow (~870-name small/mid-cap) tier: a large share of small-cap-driven backtest edge is a microcap artifact. Combined with the repo's own survivorship caveat (21 of 22 major 2020s delistings absent), overflow avgR should be treated as an upper bound and haircut hardest.

base_rates.claim: 215 alternative-beta strategies marketed by global investment banks: median 73% deterioration in Sharpe ratio from backtest to live period; the most complex strategies' live-vs-backtest Sharpe reduction exceeds the simplest strategies' by more than 30 percentage points. (NOTE: the assignment's 'live Sharpe ~ half of backtest' understates this paper; the reported MEDIAN is a 73% cut, i.e. live Sharpe roughly a quarter to a third of backtest.)
base_rates.number: -73% median Sharpe; complexity penalty >30 pp
base_rates.source: Suhonen, Lennkh & Perez, Journal of Portfolio Management 43(2) 2017, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2757113
base_rates.applicability: Base rate for strategies designed by sell-side quants with strong incentives to overfit; this book is closer to that population than to academic factors in ONE respect (many parameters, many overlays added the same year, some explicitly shipped as appetite decisions), but unlike bank products it has been traded by its designer and has pre-registration discipline. Use 73% as the pessimistic tail, not the central case.

base_rates.claim: ETF index strategies delivered ~5%/yr excess return in the pre-launch backtest and ~0% live after launch.
base_rates.number: ~+5%/yr backtest -> ~0% live
base_rates.source: Brightman, Li & Liu (Research Affiliates), 'Chasing Performance with ETFs' 2015, https://www.researchaffiliates.com/publications/articles/626-live-from-newport-beach-its-smart-beta
base_rates.applicability: Selection-on-backtest base rate. Relevant to any strategy in the book that was ADDED because its recent cell looked good (pilots launched 2026-07/08); launch timing after a strong run predicts worse live results.

base_rates.claim: Smart-beta index market-adjusted return falls from +2.77%/yr before ETF listing to -0.44%/yr after listing (from ~+3% 'on paper' to about -0.5% to -1% live); the drop is not explained by factor-premium variation, timing, or diminishing returns to scale, i.e. it is data mining in index construction.
base_rates.source: Huang, Song & Xiang, 'The Smart Beta Mirage', JFQA 59(6) 2024, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3622753
base_rates.applicability: Corroborates the launch-selection effect with a published, peer-reviewed sample. The mechanism (parameter search until the backtest looks good) is exactly what a grid search over thresholds/ATR multiples/hold days produces; strategies whose parameters were tuned on the full ledger should carry the larger end of the haircut range.

base_rates.claim: 1,726 commercially distributed structured strategies from 10 institutions: volatility-adjusted return (10% vol target) is 3.6% p.a. in the 6 months before launch vs 1.5% live (-2.1 pp), and 4.1% vs 1.0% over 12 months (-3.1 pp); commodities decay -4.0/-4.6 pp, FX -4.6/-3.5 pp; strategies launched after unusually strong factor conditions deteriorate materially more.
base_rates.number: -2.1 pp (6m), -3.1 pp (12m) at 10% vol, i.e. ~60-75% of vol-adjusted return lost
base_rates.source: arXiv 2604.18821, 'Evaluating Structured Strategy Backtests: Peer Benchmarks, Regime Timing, and Live Performance', 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18821
base_rates.applicability: Most recent and largest sample; the 60-75% loss of vol-adjusted return in the first live year matches Suhonen's 73% and is the current best estimate for sell-side-style products. The regime-timing finding maps onto the repo's own observation that marginal-leg edge is episode-concentrated.

base_rates.claim: 888 retail/quant algorithms with >= 6 months out-of-sample: backtest Sharpe ratio explains almost none of out-of-sample Sharpe (R2 < 0.025); the more backtests a developer ran, the larger the in-sample vs out-of-sample gap; volatility, max drawdown, hedging and higher moments predicted OOS better (ML model R2 = 0.17).
base_rates.number: R2 < 0.025 (IS Sharpe -> OOS Sharpe); R2 0.17 with risk features
base_rates.source: Wiecki, Campbell, Lent & Stauth (Quantopian), Journal of Investing 2016, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2745220
base_rates.applicability: The number-of-backtests result is the operational version of the deflated-Sharpe logic: the repo's negative-results registry (dozens of rejected variants, ML layer, tilt studies) is the trial count N that inflates the surviving strategies' apparent edge. Also argues for sizing off risk features (vol, drawdown depth) rather than backtest Sharpe rank when allocating across the 15 strategies.

base_rates.claim: Multiple-testing haircut on Sharpe ratios is nonlinear: high Sharpe/t-stat strategies are only moderately penalized, marginal ones (t near 2) are heavily penalized (haircuts of 52-75% in the paper's worked examples); a t-ratio of 3.0 is the proposed single-test hurdle given >= 316 tested factors, and a flat 50% haircut is 'a serious mistake'.
base_rates.number: t > 3.0 hurdle; example haircuts 52.0%, 67.3%, 71.3%, 74.6%; 316 factors
base_rates.source: Harvey & Liu, 'Backtesting', Journal of Portfolio Management 2015, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2345489; Harvey, Liu & Zhu, RFS 2016
base_rates.applicability: Supports DIFFERENTIATED haircuts inside the book: strategies with clustered t > 3 over 20+ years (OLV, OVS, FAMILY4 core) get a small statistical haircut; pilots and overlays with clustered t in the 1.5-2.2 range (3x Leader Gap Fade t = 2.17, FAMILY4 frag band t = -1.96, cycle tilt ~1.5 sigma) are in the zone where the multiple-testing haircut approaches 60-100%.

base_rates.claim: Expected maximum Sharpe ratio of N zero-edge independent trials: E[max SR] ~ (1-g) Z^-1(1-1/N) + g Z^-1(1-1/(N e)), g = 0.5772; with only 5 years of data, no more than ~45 independent configurations can be tried before the best one is expected to show an in-sample annualized Sharpe of 1.0 with expected OOS Sharpe of 0. Computed for this book's 23-year sample: E[max annualized SR] = 0.33 (N=10), 0.53 (N=100), 0.68 (N=1000); MinBTL to keep E[max SR] = 1 is 2.5y (N=10), 5.0y (N=45), 6.4y (N=100), 10.6y (N=1000).
base_rates.source: Bailey & Lopez de Prado, 'The Deflated Sharpe Ratio', JPM 2014, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2460551; Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado & Zhu, Notices of the AMS 2014, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2308659; own calculation from the published formulas
base_rates.applicability: With 23 years of daily data, even 1,000 trials cannot manufacture a whole-book Sharpe of 2 from noise (noise ceiling ~0.7), so the PURE selection-bias haircut on the book-level Sharpe is bounded at roughly 0.5-0.7 Sharpe points. The bulk of any realistic decay is therefore structural (crowding, regime, costs, survivorship), which the 26-73% empirical base rates capture and the DSR does not. For a single pilot with 3-5 years of live-relevant data, the same formulas say a handful of tried variants already produce in-sample Sharpe ~1 by luck.

base_rates.claim: Minimum track record length (95% confidence that true annual Sharpe > SR*, daily observations): to reject SR* = 0 takes 0.7y at SR 2.0, 1.2y at SR 1.5, 2.7y at SR 1.0, 5.5y at SR 0.7; to reject SR* = 0.5 takes 1.2y (SR 2.0), 2.7y (SR 1.5), 10.9y (SR 1.0), 68y (SR 0.7). Negative skew (-1) with kurtosis 6 adds ~10%.
base_rates.number: 1.2-2.7y to separate SR 1.5-2.0 from 0.5; 11y to separate 1.0 from 0.5
base_rates.source: Bailey & Lopez de Prado, 'The Sharpe Ratio Efficient Frontier', Journal of Risk 2012, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1821643; own calculation from the PSR/MinTRL formula
base_rates.applicability: A 1-3 year live record can only tell you whether the live Sharpe is above zero, not whether it is 1.0 vs 0.7. Live records of that length should be used as a KILL criterion (live Sharpe < 0 or drawdown far outside the backtest distribution), not as a re-estimation input that overrides the haircut backtest prior.

base_rates.claim: At 30 trades with avgR +0.5 and sd(R) 1.5 (typical book cell), the per-trade t-stat is 1.78 and the 95% CI on per-trade Sharpe is [-0.03, 0.70]; at 50 trades t = 2.29, CI [0.05, 0.62]; at 100 trades t = 3.24. A pilot cannot clear the Harvey-Liu t > 3 hurdle before ~100 trades unless avgR is far above book norms.
base_rates.source: Own calculation (Lo 2002 Sharpe SE = sqrt((1+SR^2/2)/n)), consistent with Harvey & Liu 2015 hurdle
base_rates.applicability: Quantifies category (b): a <30-trade pilot sits below the single-test threshold, and in a multiple-testing frame (many pilots tried, negative registry) its haircut under Harvey-Liu is close to total; sizing must come from the prior (family analogy) plus a small credit for pre-registration, not from the pilot's own numbers.

base_rates.claim: Century-long, six-asset-class factor evidence: estimated premia drop ~30% out of sample versus the original discovery samples, which the authors attribute more to overfitting than to informed trading; factor-timing strategies show only modest predictability that fails to survive lags and costs.
base_rates.number: -30% OOS premia
base_rates.source: Ilmanen, Israel, Lee, Moskowitz & Thapar (AQR), Journal of Investment Management 2021, https://www.aqr.com/Insights/Research/Journal-Article/How-Do-Factor-Premia-Vary-Over-Time-A-Century-of-Evidence
base_rates.applicability: Best base rate for ROBUST, simple, low-turnover edges: ~30% haircut. The book's simplest, oldest rules (index dip-buys, OVS-style vol-spike fades) belong near this end; the timing result is a caution against expecting dial-based sizing to add much after costs and lags, consistent with the repo's failed book-wide throttle.

base_rates.claim: Bayesian replication study: ~85% of factors replicate (US and global); post-publication alpha decline of the McLean-Pontiff magnitude is what a Bayesian posterior formed from published evidence predicts, though observed attenuation is 'somewhat stronger' than the model; factors with higher in-sample alpha still have higher out-of-sample alpha (rank information survives, level does not).
base_rates.number: 85% replicate; decay ~consistent with posterior shrinkage
base_rates.source: Jensen, Kelly & Pedersen, Journal of Finance 2023, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3774514
base_rates.applicability: Justifies allocating MORE to strategies with stronger backtests (rank survives) while haircutting all LEVELS; i.e. cross-strategy allocation can lean on backtest ordering even though absolute expectancy should be shrunk 30-50%.

base_rates.claim: Factor investing 'three blunders': backtests overstate live returns via data mining, crowding and unrealistic cost assumptions; downside shocks are far larger than backtests imply; and factor diversification vanishes when factor returns correlate in stress.
base_rates.number: Qualitative (award-winning survey; no single decay number)
base_rates.source: Arnott, Harvey, Kalesnik & Linnainmaa, 'Alice's Adventures in Factorland', JPM 2019, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3331680
base_rates.applicability: The third blunder is the one this book is most exposed to: 15 strategies whose backtest Sharpe ~2 depends on low cross-strategy correlation; the repo's own worst-day analysis (-15.75% NAV uncapped, entire maxDD in one day) shows the correlation collapse already exists in-sample. Book-level Sharpe should be haircut at least as much as strategy-level Sharpe, not less.

base_rates.claim: Classic short-term (1-month) reversal: trading costs are driven by excessive trading in small caps; restricting to large caps and lowering turnover leaves 30-50 bps/week net (1990-2009 sample, 100 largest names: 16.25%/yr net, Sharpe 1.09, maxDD -53%). By 2023 the classic reversal effect 'has steadily weakened over time, to the point of now having vanished entirely in most regions'; composite short-term signals (reversal + short-term momentum + revisions + risk + seasonality) still show significant net alpha out-of-sample and post-publication.
base_rates.number: 30-50 bps/week net large-cap (2011); classic reversal ~0 by 2023
base_rates.source: de Groot, Huij & Zhou, Journal of Banking & Finance 2012, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1605049; Blitz, Hanauer, Honarvar, Huisman & van Vliet, Financial Analysts Journal 2023, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4115411; Quantpedia summary https://quantpedia.com/strategies/short-term-reversal-in-stocks
base_rates.applicability: Direct for the dip-buy and low-volume-oversold families: unconditional reversal in liquid US names is a dead base rate, but CONDITIONED short-horizon signals (which is what OLV/seasonal dip-buys are) retain edge. Expect the unconditional component of any dip-buy to be worth ~0 and the conditional component to carry a 30-45% haircut, and expect small-cap reversal to lose most of its gross edge to costs.

base_rates.claim: Reversal-strategy returns are the return to liquidity provision: they fell steadily to under 0.2%/day by 2007 (from ~1%/day in the 1998 LTCM and 2000-01 episodes), then spiked above LTCM levels in 2008; the VIX is a far stronger predictor of reversal returns than lagged market returns, and conditional Sharpe ratios rise 'enormously' with the VIX.
base_rates.source: Nagel, 'Evaporating Liquidity', Review of Financial Studies 2012, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1988706
base_rates.applicability: Outside evidence for dialing single-stock mean-reversion sizing UP in high-VIX tape (signal quality rises with volatility), which is the OPPOSITE of the book's FAMILY4 0.25x band at high fragility. The two are reconcilable because FAMILY4 is index/ETF beta-long dip-buying while Nagel's construct is market-neutral cross-sectional liquidity provision; the evidence supports treating the OLV-style single-name legs and any market-neutral reversal differently from beta-long dip-buys in stress.

base_rates.claim: Anomalies with > 50% monthly turnover rarely generate significant net spreads; average execution cost of mid-turnover anomalies is 20-57 bps per trade; capacity for new capital is inversely related to turnover, with size/value/profitability having the most capacity and short-horizon strategies the least.
base_rates.number: 20-57 bps/trade; >50%/mo turnover rarely survives
base_rates.source: Novy-Marx & Velikov, Review of Financial Studies 2016, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2535173
base_rates.applicability: This book's 1-63 day holds put it in the high-turnover class where capacity is smallest and cost sensitivity highest; overflow small-cap fills at 2-5x the spread cost of liquid names should be modeled explicitly before scaling that tier.

base_rates.claim: 52-week-high momentum (George & Hwang 2004) remains robust in price momentum's post-publication record across markets, but the 52-week-high strategy on liquid international stocks 'fails to produce significant dollar profits once short-sale restrictions, transaction costs and liquidity constraints are accounted for'; momentum generally is the most robust post-publication factor (Jensen et al. 2023; Ilmanen et al. 2021).
base_rates.number: Momentum: most robust post-publication factor; 52wh liquid-only net profits not significant (intl)
base_rates.source: George & Hwang, Journal of Finance 2004; Liu, Liu & Ma, Journal of International Money and Finance 2011, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0261560610001099
base_rates.applicability: For the 52wh Breakout / Sector BO strategies: the underlying anomaly has the best out-of-sample survival record in the literature, arguing for the LOWER end of the haircut range on the signal, but net-of-cost edge in a liquid-only universe is thin, arguing against scaling notional aggressively.

base_rates.claim: Missing CRSP delisting returns for performance-related delistings average about -30% (NYSE/AMEX) and about -55% (Nasdaq); after correcting the Nasdaq delisting bias 'there is no evidence that there ever was a size effect on Nasdaq'. Delisting firm-years cluster in the lowest decile of anomaly sorts, so anomaly returns change materially when they are included (Beaver, McNichols & Price 2007).
base_rates.number: -30% (NYSE/AMEX), -55% (Nasdaq) missing delisting returns
base_rates.source: Shumway, Journal of Finance 1997, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1997.tb03818.x; Shumway & Warther, Journal of Finance 1999; Beaver, McNichols & Price, JAE 2007, https://www.ssrn.com/abstract=949601
base_rates.applicability: Direct for overflow LONG strategies (oversold dip-buys, OLV on small caps): the names absent from a survivor-only universe are disproportionately the ones that WERE oversold and then delisted, so survivor-only backtests overstate long dip-buy expectancy specifically. For overflow SHORT strategies (OVS) the bias runs the other way (missing losers would have been winning shorts), so the survivorship haircut should be asymmetric.

base_rates.claim: Survivor-only backtests of a small-cap universe inflate annual returns by 4.94 pp (23.3% relative) and Sharpe by 0.097 (9.1% relative) versus a point-in-time universe; 82.5% of names left the index over 9 years (16.1% delisted). CRSP survivor-biased vs survivorship-free annualized returns: 9.0% vs 7.4% (1926-2001). Mutual-fund survivorship bias ~0.9%/yr (Elton-Gruber-Blake); hedge-fund backfill bias 1.4%/yr (Fung & Hsieh 2000).
base_rates.number: +4.94 pp/yr (+23% relative) small-cap; +1.6 pp/yr CRSP; +0.9 to +1.4 pp/yr funds
base_rates.source: Ranse, 'Survivorship Bias in Emerging Market Small-Cap Indices', SSRN 2025/26, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstractid=5833162; CRSP comparison as cited in industry summaries; Fung & Hsieh, Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 2000, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1414464
base_rates.applicability: Quantifies the survivorship component of the overflow haircut: a 20-25% relative overstatement of return for a buy-and-hold small-cap universe is a floor; for a strategy that selects on weakness (dip-buys) the overstatement is larger because selection concentrates in the names most likely to have been removed.

base_rates.claim: Practitioner rule (Carver, ex-AHL): size positions as if the Sharpe ratio is HALF the backtest/expected value, then apply half-Kelly; realistic live Sharpe expectations of 0.5-1.0 for a diversified systematic book, and 'for other people you should expect much less'.
base_rates.number: 0.5 x Sharpe, then 0.5 Kelly = 25% of backtest full-Kelly vol target
base_rates.source: Carver, 'Systematic Trading' (Harriman House) 2015; https://qoppac.blogspot.com/2020/03/how-much-risk-should-we-take.html
base_rates.applicability: An outside benchmark for the principal's '6% of backtest full Kelly': Carver's rule lands at ~25% of backtest full Kelly (after a 50% Sharpe haircut and half-Kelly). The current 6% is ~4x more conservative than that rule; even a 73% Suhonen-style haircut with half-Kelly gives ~13%. The evidence supports a higher overall fraction than 6% if drawdown is not the binding constraint, PROVIDED the book-level Sharpe 2 is first haircut to the 1.0-1.3 range.

base_rates.claim: Short-volatility strategies that performed well pre-2018 deteriorated afterward as volatility became better priced and quant participation grew; no peer-reviewed backtest-vs-live base rate exists specifically for leveraged-ETF fades or intraday vol-spike shorts (gap in the evidence).
base_rates.number: No numeric base rate available; post-2018 deterioration reported qualitatively
base_rates.source: arXiv 2403.00474 (2024) and practitioner literature, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.00474
base_rates.applicability: Flag: the OVS / 3x-ETF fade family has no external decay base rate; treat it with the generic 35-50% haircut and lean on the book's own out-of-sample record (these strategies have the longest live histories in the book) rather than outside evidence.

implications_for_this_book: RECOMMENDED HAIRCUT (a) — mature strategy, 15-20y backtest, 1-3y live: shrink backtest expectancy (avgR and Sharpe) by 35-50% as the central case (range 25-60%). Anchors: 26% (McLean-Pontiff pure OOS) and ~30% (Ilmanen et al.) as the floor for simple, old rules; 43% (Falck-Rej-Thesmar) as the published-anomaly mean; 58-73% (McLean-Pontiff post-pub, Suhonen, 2026 structured-strategy sample) as the ceiling for crowded or complex rules. Place each strategy inside the range by (i) rule age and simplicity (older/simpler -> 25-35%), (ii) clustered t-stat (t > 3 -> low end; t 2-3 -> mid; t < 2 -> treat as pilot), (iii) how much of its ledger edge is in one or two episodes (episode-concentrated -> high end), and (iv) how close the signal is to a textbook anomaly in liquid US names (plain reversal / 52wh -> high end).

The 1-3 year live record should be used as a kill/confirm gate, not a re-estimation input. MinTRL math: 1.2-2.7 years separates a live Sharpe of 1.5-2.0 from 0.5, but 11 years separates 1.0 from 0.5. Precision-weighting a 2-year live Sharpe (SE ~0.85) against a 20-year backtest (SE ~0.27, inflated to ~0.5 for nonstationarity) gives the live record 10-25% weight. Practical rule: live record can only move a strategy's sizing by about +/-25% around the haircut prior, unless it triggers a kill (live Sharpe < 0 over >= 2 years, or realized drawdown beyond the backtest's worst by > 1.5x).

RECOMMENDED HAIRCUT (b) — pilot with < 30 trades: 60-80% haircut on the pilot's own backtest expectancy, implemented as a risk budget of 25-40% of what a mature strategy with the same family profile gets, stepping up on TRADE COUNT not calendar time (e.g. 0.3x until 30 trades, 0.5x at 50 trades and clustered t > 2, 0.75x at 100 trades and t > 2.5, full at t > 3 or a comparable pre-registered LOYO floor). Rationale: at n = 30 a book-typical cell (avgR 0.5, sd 1.5) has t = 1.78 and a 95% CI touching zero; Harvey-Liu haircuts approach 100% for marginal t under multiple testing; the repo's own negative registry is the trial count N that Wiecki et al. show widens the IS/OOS gap; Suhonen/Falck show complexity and recency decay hardest, and every pilot in this book is by definition recent. Credit pre-registration and episode-clustered validation (3x Leader Gap Fade t = 2.17, LOYO 1.55, Monthly Weak Close t = 4.08 on N = 15 fills) only as movement WITHIN the 25-40% band, not as an exit from it. Applies to: 3x Leader Gap Fade, Monthly Weak Close, 3x Bear Fade (one-regime sample), the event sleeve trades, and every overlay/tilt shipped in 2026 with N < 30 conditional trades.

RECOMMENDED HAIRCUT (c) — overflow small-cap tier with survivorship exposure: an ADDITIONAL 20-35% cut on top of (a), compounding to a 50-65% total haircut on ledger avgR for overflow LONG strategies (OLV, LT Trend ST OS, St OS Sznl, 52wh Breakout on overflow), until the point-in-time universe lands. Components: survivor-only small-cap universes overstate returns 20-25% relative for buy-and-hold and more for weakness-selecting strategies (Shumway -30%/-55% missing delisting returns cluster in the lowest anomaly deciles; Beaver et al.); 65-82% of anomalies fail once microcaps are neutralized (Hou-Xue-Zhang); small-cap reversal edge is mostly consumed by trading costs (de Groot; Novy-Marx-Velikov 20-57 bps/trade). For overflow SHORT strategies (OVS) the survivorship sign reverses (missing delisted names would have been winning shorts), so apply only the tier's cost/borrow haircut (~10-20% extra), not the survivorship cut. In sizing terms: keep overflow long per-signal risk at <= 0.5x of the liquid-tier equivalent (the existing OLV 35->25 bps override is roughly in this range; consider extending the same ratio to the other overflow-eligible longs).

Book-level Kelly fraction: with the book Sharpe haircut from ~2.0 to ~1.0-1.3 (35-50% cut), the DSR noise ceiling for 23 years of daily data is only ~0.5-0.7 Sharpe even at 1,000 trials, so the haircut is structural rather than statistical and should not be doubled up with a separate multiple-testing haircut at the book level. Carver's practitioner rule (half the Sharpe, half Kelly) implies ~25% of BACKTEST full Kelly; a Suhonen-pessimistic version (27% of backtest Sharpe, half Kelly) implies ~13%. The current ~6% is below both; if drawdown is not the binding constraint, the outside evidence supports moving toward 10-20% of backtest full Kelly (equivalently ~25-50% of the HAIRCUT full Kelly), scaled in over time and with the per-strategy 250 bps/day cap retained as the sole tail bound.

Cross-strategy allocation can lean on backtest RANK (Jensen-Kelly-Pedersen: higher in-sample alpha still predicts higher out-of-sample alpha) even though LEVELS are shrunk; but Wiecki et al. found backtest Sharpe rank had near-zero OOS predictive power for retail algos while vol/drawdown features did. Net: allocate by a blend of haircut expectancy and realized risk profile (drawdown depth, tail behaviour), and avoid allocating on raw backtest Sharpe alone.

Haircut the fitted OVERLAYS (frag bands, P/C fear bands, cycle tilts, recency ladders, gap derates) harder than the base rules: they are recent, parameter-rich, and several were shipped as appetite decisions or on t ~ 1.5-2 evidence. Falck-Rej-Thesmar's complexity finding and Ilmanen's factor-timing result both say timing/conditioning layers rarely survive lags and costs. Where an overlay REDUCES size (0.25x bands, derates) the haircut argues for keeping it (it lowers variance either way); where it INCREASES size (the 1.25x fear-ON boost) the haircut argues for treating the boost as unproven and capping it at 1.0x until the post-ship review passes.

Signal-quality timing that the outside evidence DOES support: single-name mean-reversion (liquidity-provision) returns and conditional Sharpe rise sharply with VIX (Nagel), so OLV-type legs have a defensible case for sizing UP in high-VIX tape, whereas beta-long index dip-buys do not (the repo's FAMILY4 PIT result). Any dial-up should be conditioned on realized/implied vol of the traded name and be market-neutral in construction, not on the composite fragility dial.

Strategy-family haircut priors, for the orchestrator to combine with in-repo evidence: index/ETF dip-buys and vol-spike fades (old, simple, most live history) 25-35%; OLV and conditioned single-name reversals 35-45% (classic reversal is dead, conditioned reversal survives); 52wh/sector breakouts 30-40% on signal (momentum is the most robust factor) but with explicit cost modeling because net-of-cost 52wh profits in liquid universes are thin; 3x-ETF fades and bear-ETF fades 40-55% (one-regime samples, no external base rate, short-vol deterioration post-2018); every 2026 pilot per (b); overflow longs per (c).

Launch-timing effect (Brightman et al., Huang et al., 2026 structured sample): strategies added right after a strong run of their own cell decay worst. Any strategy or overlay added because its recent 1-3 year cell looked exceptional should start at the low end of its family's sizing band and earn its way up on trade count.
contested_points: How much of decay is statistical vs arbitrage: McLean-Pontiff attribute 26 of 58 pts to data mining and 32 to informed trading; Chen-Zimmermann put publication bias at only 12% and mispricing correction at 35%; Ilmanen et al. attribute their 30% OOS drop mostly to overfitting; Falck-Rej-Thesmar find overfitting proxies and publication recency dominate while arbitrage variables are marginal; Jensen-Kelly-Pedersen say the observed decay is roughly what Bayesian shrinkage predicts. For an unpublished private book the practical consequence is a wide central band (25-60%) rather than a point estimate.

Flat 50% haircut vs differentiated haircut: Harvey-Liu call a uniform 50% cut 'a serious mistake' (nonlinear, t-dependent haircut instead); Carver and much of practice use the flat halving; Suhonen's sell-side sample shows a MEDIAN cut of 73%, worse than the flat rule. The assignment brief's 'live Sharpe ~ half of backtest' for Suhonen et al. understates that paper.

Backtest Sharpe as an allocation signal: Wiecki et al. (retail algos) find R2 < 0.025 between IS and OOS Sharpe, while Jensen-Kelly-Pedersen (academic factors) find in-sample alpha rank does carry into out-of-sample alpha. The populations differ (thousands of overfit hobbyist algos vs replicated factors); this book is closer to the latter in discipline but to the former in parameter count.

Is short-term reversal dead or merely time-varying? Blitz et al. 2023 say the classic effect has vanished in most regions; Nagel 2012 says reversal returns are liquidity-provision returns that collapse in calm tape and explode in high-VIX episodes; de Groot et al. show net edge survives in large caps at 30-50 bps/week (2011 sample). The reconciliation (unconditional edge ~0, conditional edge alive) is an inference, not a measured base rate.

Sign of the survivorship haircut is strategy-direction dependent (longs overstated, shorts understated); no paper quantifies the short-side understatement, so the asymmetric recommendation in (c) is reasoned rather than measured.

The DSR/MinBTL computations assume independent trials and normal returns; correlated trials (parameter neighbours) reduce the effective N and the selection haircut, while fat tails and the fitted overlays' in-sample dependence on the same ledger push the other way. Neither correction is quantified here.

Sizing up in high-VIX tape for single-name reversal (Nagel) conflicts on its face with the repo's FAMILY4 0.25x high-fragility band (PIT t = -1.96); the two constructs differ (market-neutral liquidity provision vs beta-long index dip-buys), but the book has not tested the market-neutral version, so the dial-up is a hypothesis, not a base rate.

The 'Not All Factors Crowd Equally' alpha-decay paper (arXiv 2512.11913, hyperbolic decay, reversal crash probability 1.7-1.8x when crowded) has been withdrawn for revision by its authors and should not be relied on.

outside_evidence.topic: Kelly and growth-optimal sizing in practice: Thorp's practice, the estimation-error case for fractional Kelly, drawdown-constrained Kelly (Grossman-Zhou 1993; Busseti-Ryu-Boyd 2016), Kelly under leverage/margin limits, how multi-strategy pod shops size and cut, and the Sharpe -> Kelly-leverage mapping with credible ex-ante Sharpe levels. Applied to a 15-strategy short-horizon US equity book (backtest Sharpe ~2, ~4,700 trades 2003-2026, running at ~6% of backtest full Kelly on a flat $750k base, IBKR portfolio margin).

base_rates.claim: Continuous-time Kelly: full-Kelly leverage L* = (m-r)/s^2 = Sharpe/vol; max growth g = r + S^2/2 depends only on the Sharpe ratio. At fraction c of Kelly, growth = (S^2/2)*c(2-c) and portfolio vol = c*S. Half Kelly keeps 3/4 of max growth.
base_rates.source: Thorp, 'The Kelly Criterion in Blackjack, Sports Betting and the Stock Market', Handbook of Asset and Liability Management (2006), eq. 7.3 and Sec. 7.3; Rotando & Thorp, Amer. Math. Monthly (1992)
base_rates.applicability: With backtest Sharpe 2.0, full Kelly is a 200%-annualized-vol book. Running at c=0.06 implies ~12% annualized vol and ~23%/yr flat growth in the GBM model, which cross-checks the repo's own numbers (~$157k/yr on $750k = 21%, Sharpe 1.85 => ~11% vol, GRM replay). The book sits deep in the linear part of the growth curve (Sharpe near-invariant to GRM 1.0-1.75 is exactly what the model predicts at small c): every doubling of size roughly doubles growth until c approaches ~0.25 of TRUE Kelly.

base_rates.claim: Drawdown probability at fractional Kelly (GBM, infinite horizon): P(wealth ever falls to fraction x of start) = x^(2/c - 1). At full Kelly P(ever halve) = 1/2 and P(double before halving) = 2/3; at half Kelly P(ever halve) = 1/8 and P(double before halve) = 8/9.
base_rates.source: Thorp (2006) eq. 7.9-7.13; MacLean, Thorp & Ziemba, Quantitative Finance 10(7):681-687 (2010) (blackjack table: P[double before halve] 0.999 at 0.1 Kelly, 0.67 at full Kelly)
base_rates.applicability: These are GBM numbers (no fat tails, no gap risk) and are the right order of magnitude only for the MEDIAN path. They say a book at 6% of a TRUE Sharpe-2 Kelly is over-insured against drawdown by orders of magnitude (P(-20%) ~ 0.07%), and that even 25% of true Kelly has only ~21% lifetime odds of a 20% drawdown. But the exponent is 2/c - 1 on the TRUE Kelly fraction, so a 2x Sharpe overestimate halves the exponent (c_true = 2 c_bt) and a 4x overestimate quarters it: the repo's 6% is 12-24% of true Kelly if the live Sharpe is 1.0-0.5, and the 20% drawdown odds move from 0.07% to 3-19%.

base_rates.claim: Estimation error is the practitioner reason for fractional Kelly. Overbetting is penalized far more than underbetting: at 2x Kelly growth is zero; overestimating edge by more than 2x turns full-Kelly growth negative. Thorp: 'overbetting is much more severely penalized than using too small an f'.
base_rates.number: Growth at 2x Kelly = 0 (=r); Benter: edge overestimate >2x -> negative growth, 'easily done in practice'; Thorp fig. 5: if true mean = 0.5 x estimated, half Kelly is exactly optimal (zero loss), full Kelly loses 25% of achievable growth, 1.5x Kelly is a 'disaster'.
base_rates.source: Thorp (2006) Sec. 7.3; Benter, 'Computer Based Horse Race Handicapping and Wagering Systems' (1994), in Efficiency of Racetrack Betting Markets; MacLean-Thorp-Ziemba (2010)
base_rates.applicability: The relevant question for this book is not 'how far under Kelly' but 'Kelly of WHAT Sharpe'. Half Kelly is the growth-optimal choice if you believe the live edge is half the backtest (Thorp's fig. 5), quarter Kelly if you believe it is a quarter. With published live-vs-backtest decay of 50-73% (below), the defensible target fraction of BACKTEST Kelly is 0.25-0.5 x (deflation factor 0.25-0.5) = roughly 6-25% of backtest Kelly. The current 6% is the bottom of that band, i.e. it already embeds a ~4x Sharpe haircut AND a half-Kelly safety factor stacked on top.

base_rates.claim: Shrinkage Kelly under parameter uncertainty (Baker-McHale): the optimal fraction of Kelly shrinks with the uncertainty of the edge estimate; a widely-used closed form is alpha = SR_edge^2/(SR_edge^2 + 1) where SR_edge = estimated edge / its standard error (i.e. its t-stat scaled). Uncertainty in means matters ~10x more than uncertainty in variances.
base_rates.number: Chopra & Ziemba (1993): cash-equivalent loss from errors in means : variances : covariances ~ 20 : 2 : 1. Baker-McHale (2013): shrunken Kelly beats raw Kelly out of sample in simulation and tennis-betting data; shrinkage grows with sigma of the probability estimate.
base_rates.source: Baker & McHale, Decision Analysis 10(3):189-199 (2013); Chopra & Ziemba, J. Portfolio Management (1993) as cited in MacLean-Thorp-Ziemba (2010); LessWrong 'Never go full Kelly' derivation of alpha = SR^2/(SR^2+1)
base_rates.applicability: For a book with ~4,700 trades and a 23-year backtest, the naive standard error on Sharpe is ~1/sqrt(23) ~ 0.21, so the sampling-error shrinkage alone is small (alpha ~0.9 at Sharpe 2). The binding uncertainty is NOT sampling error, it is selection/overfitting and regime non-stationarity, which these formulas do not capture. Per-strategy, the sampling-error shrinkage is material: a strategy with 30 trades and t~2 gets alpha ~ 4/(4+1) = 0.8, one with t~1.4 gets ~0.66. This argues for allocating risk across strategies in proportion to (per-strategy Sharpe x shrinkage), not equal risk, and for the pilot-tier discount already used for 3x Leader Gap Fade / Monthly Weak Close.

base_rates.claim: Drawdown-constrained Kelly (Grossman-Zhou): to never lose more than fraction alpha of the running peak, invest full-Kelly leverage applied to the excess of wealth over the floor (alpha x running max), i.e. exposure = L* x (W - alpha M). Exposure shrinks linearly as drawdown approaches the floor and re-expands as wealth makes new highs. Klass-Nowicki (2005) show it is not optimal in discrete time.
base_rates.number: Exposure = (m-r)/s^2 x (W - alpha x M_t); at the floor, exposure -> 0. Growth rate is reduced by factor (1 - alpha) relative to unconstrained Kelly in the GZ continuous solution.
base_rates.source: Grossman & Zhou, Mathematical Finance 3:241-276 (1993); Cvitanic & Karatzas (1995); Klass & Nowicki, Statistics & Probability Letters (2005)
base_rates.applicability: This is the theoretically clean form of a 'drawdown-triggered cut': a CONTINUOUS de-lever toward a floor, not a step cut at 5%/7.5%. Because the principal explicitly does not want a drawdown constraint, the GZ result is mainly useful as a benchmark: any drawdown-cut rule the study considers should be scored against the GZ cost (growth x (1-alpha)) and against the negative Kaminski-Lo result for mean-reverting P&L (below).

base_rates.claim: Risk-constrained Kelly (Busseti-Ryu-Boyd): maximize growth subject to P(min wealth < alpha) < beta, made convex via E[(return)^(-lambda)] <= 1 with lambda = log(beta)/log(alpha). The bound is close to Monte Carlo drawdown risk, and at equal drawdown risk the RCK bet grows faster than fractional Kelly.
base_rates.number: Finite-outcome example (alpha=0.7, beta=0.1): Kelly growth 0.062 with actual P(drawdown to 0.7) = 0.397; RCK growth 0.047 at actual risk 0.099; fractional Kelly at the same ~0.10 risk grows ~0.035 -> RCK ~34% higher growth. Continuous-return example: Kelly 0.077 growth at 0.569 risk; RCK 0.043 at 0.101.
base_rates.source: Busseti, Ryu & Boyd, 'Risk-Constrained Kelly Gambling', Journal of Investing 25(3):118-134 (2016), arXiv:1603.06183
base_rates.applicability: Two takeaways. (1) Even the risk-constrained optimum accepts a 10% chance of a 30% drawdown while giving up only ~25-45% of full-Kelly growth, i.e. real growth-optimal sizing tolerates drawdowns far larger than this book has ever run (max -12.6% NAV at GRM 1.5). (2) Uniform fractional Kelly is inefficient: RCK cuts the bets with the worst tail per unit of growth (here: no-stop OLV stacks, 3x-ETF fades, gap-through shorts) and keeps bets with bounded downside near full size. That is an argument for heterogeneous scaling across the 15 strategies rather than one GRM.

base_rates.claim: Kelly under leverage/margin limits: the optimum is the unconstrained Kelly point if feasible, else the constraint binds and you sit at the cap. Thorp warns the GBM math ignores jumps: in Oct 1987 the S&P fell 23% in a day; a 2x-levered book would have jumped to 2.85x before any rebalance. Reg T caps initial equity leverage at 2x; portfolio margin ~6.67x (15% stress).
base_rates.number: Thorp's Berkshire example: unconstrained f* = 6.22x; 'conservative' f = 2.0 (the customer max at the time) gives g = 0.295 vs g = 0.495 at 6.22x. IBKR portfolio margin: +/-15% stress -> ~6.67x max on stock. Multi-manager platforms report ~4-8x gross per fundamental pod, ~5.7x (Citadel) / ~6.7x (Millennium) fund-level gross (2023).
base_rates.source: Thorp (2006) Sec. 7 and Sec. 8; Interactive Brokers portfolio-margin documentation; hedgefundinterview.com 'Pod Shop Risk Limits' (2023-2025 reporting)
base_rates.applicability: At 6% of a Sharpe-2 Kelly the book uses a small fraction of portfolio-margin capacity, so margin is not the binding constraint on a 2-4x size increase; gap risk is. The relevant leverage number for this book is GROSS NOTIONAL relative to NAV on the days OLV stacks (84% of NAV in one strategy on 2026-08-24), because a 1987-style jump is not in any GBM drawdown formula. Any sizing plan above ~25% of true Kelly needs an explicit jump-risk overlay (max gross, per-name cap) rather than relying on the x^(2/c-1) math.

base_rates.claim: What Thorp, Benter and Ziemba actually ran: fractional Kelly at roughly 1/4 to 1/2. Thorp: most people 'strongly prefer the increased safety and psychological comfort of half Kelly (or some nearby value), in exchange for giving up 1/4 of their growth rate'. Benter ran 'a conservative fractional Kelly betting strategy throughout' (1/2 or 1/3). Ziemba's lecture rule: 'when in doubt, bet less'. Pabrai bet 10% where full Kelly was 97.5% and half Kelly 38.75%.
base_rates.number: Half Kelly = 75% of max growth; third Kelly = 56%; quarter Kelly = 44%. Princeton Newport: 19.1%/yr for ~19 years, no losing year (secondary sources report 3 down months). Secondary sources disagree on Thorp's own fraction (quarter vs half).
base_rates.source: Thorp (2006) Sec. 7.3; Benter (1994); Ziemba, 'Using the Kelly Criterion for Investing' (Springer 2011, Ch. 1); MacLean-Thorp-Ziemba (2010); Poundstone 'Fortune's Formula' (2005)
base_rates.applicability: The practitioner base rate is 25-50% of the operator's HONEST edge estimate, where 'honest' already includes the practitioner's own haircut. For this book, 6% of backtest Kelly equals 25-50% of an honest Kelly only if the honest Sharpe is 0.24-0.48 (i.e. an 8x-4x haircut). If the principal believes the live Sharpe is >= 1.0 (a 2x haircut), 6% is 12% of honest Kelly, below any recorded practitioner floor, and Thorp's own math says the book is giving up ~55-65% of achievable growth for drawdown protection it does not want.

base_rates.claim: Live-vs-backtest Sharpe decay base rates: 215 bank alternative-beta strategies show a median 73% Sharpe deterioration live vs backtest (more for complex strategies, +30pp); 97 published anomalies decay 26% out-of-sample and 58% post-publication; the industry rule of thumb is a 50% Sharpe haircut and Harvey-Liu's multiple-testing framework formalizes it; a CTA-style overfitting model gives a discount factor ~2 for typical parameters; structured strategies decay from 3.6% to 1.5% vol-adjusted return (6 months) and 4.1% to 1.0% (12 months) live vs pro-forma.
base_rates.number: Median -73% (Suhonen et al. 2017); -26% OOS / -58% post-pub (McLean-Pontiff 2016); 50% haircut rule (Harvey-Liu 2015); OFF ~2 (Bouchaud et al. arXiv:1902.01802, 2019); -58% to -76% vol-adjusted (arXiv:2604.18821, 2026).
base_rates.source: Suhonen, Lennkh & Perez, J. Portfolio Management 43(2):90 (2017); McLean & Pontiff, J. Finance 71(1):5-32 (2016); Harvey & Liu, 'Backtesting', J. Portfolio Management 42(1) (2015); Bailey & Lopez de Prado, 'Deflated Sharpe Ratio' (2014); arXiv 1902.01802 (2019); arXiv 2604.18821 (2026)
base_rates.applicability: Ex ante, a backtest Sharpe of ~2 for a 15-strategy short-horizon book should be expected to realize 0.5-1.0 live (Carver's table: 'world-class systematic hedge fund' 1.5-2.0; Aurum quant-fund composite ~1.2; Millennium 2021 4.8 at fund level with hundreds of pods). The book's mitigants (23-year sample, ~4,700 trades, 15 strategies, pre-registration discipline, an already-realized live track) argue for the top of that range, not for Sharpe 2. Kelly arithmetic at Sharpe 1.0: full Kelly = 100% vol; quarter Kelly = 25% vol; the book's ~12% vol is ~12% of that Kelly.

base_rates.claim: Volatility targeting (sizing inversely to recent realized vol) raises Sharpe for risk assets and lowers left tails, but the real-time evidence is weaker than the in-sample evidence. Moreira-Muir: +25% Sharpe and 4.9% alpha for the market; Barroso & Santa-Clara: momentum Sharpe 0.53 -> 0.97 with crashes virtually eliminated; Harvey et al: Sharpe gains only for equities/credit, negligible for bonds/FX/commodities, vol-of-vol 4.6% -> 1.8%; Cederburg et al: across 103 equity strategies, implementable real-time versions generally earn LOWER Sharpe and certainty equivalents than the unmanaged strategy.
base_rates.number: Market Sharpe +25%, alpha 4.9%/yr (Moreira-Muir 2017); momentum 0.53 -> 0.97 (Barroso & Santa-Clara 2015); equity vol-of-vol 4.6% -> 1.8% (Harvey et al 2018); 103 strategies, real-time versions underperform (Cederburg et al 2020).
base_rates.source: Moreira & Muir, J. Finance (2017); Barroso & Santa-Clara, J. Financial Economics 116:111-120 (2015); Harvey, Hoyle, Korgaonkar, Rattray, Sargaison & Van Hemert, J. Portfolio Management 45(1):14 (2018); Cederburg, O'Doherty, Wang & Yan, J. Financial Economics (2020)
base_rates.applicability: The strongest result is for strategies with negative vol-return covariance and crash-prone left tails (momentum, market beta). This book already runs per-trade ATR sizing, which is asset-level vol targeting; the open question is STRATEGY-P&L-level vol targeting. The Cederburg result says do not expect a Sharpe gain from scaling book size on trailing book-P&L vol; expect at most a variance/tail benefit, and the repo's own negative results (book-wide throttle PIT t=-0.23; fragility taper -11.4R) are consistent with the real-time literature. Where the literature does support conditioning is when a SPECIFIC signal's edge is known to degrade in high-vol/crisis regimes (the FAMILY4 dip-buys at dial>=50 are that case).

base_rates.claim: Stop-loss / drawdown-cut rules add value only when P&L is positively autocorrelated (momentum or regime-switching); under a random walk a 0/1 stop rule always lowers expected return, and under mean-reverting returns the stopping premium is negative. Empirically on 1950-2004 monthly equity data, stop rules added 50-100 bp/month during stop-out periods.
base_rates.number: Random walk: stopping premium always < 0 net of the rate differential; momentum: premium proportional to serial correlation; empirical +50-100 bp/month in stopped-out months (1950-2004).
base_rates.source: Kaminski & Lo, 'When Do Stop-Loss Rules Stop Losses?', J. Financial Markets 18:234-254 (2014)
base_rates.applicability: A drawdown-triggered book-level cut is a stop-loss on the book's P&L series. It helps only if the book's daily P&L has positive autocorrelation or regime persistence (losing streaks cluster and predict more losing). Test this directly on the 23-year flat-basis daily P&L (ACF at lags 1-20, regime tests) before adopting any drawdown cut; if book P&L is mean-reverting (typical of dip-buy books: losses come in violent clusters that then recover), the cut is expected to cost money, which is what the repo's throttle studies found.

base_rates.claim: Multi-manager pod risk rules: Millennium is reported to cut a pod's capital ~50% at a 5% drawdown from allocated capital and terminate at ~7.5%; veteran PMs describe the working line as 2.5-3% from peak; Citadel/Point72 negotiate thresholds per PM; fundamental pods run ~4-8x gross, net -20% to +20%; platform-level vol targets ~8-15%; Millennium PM turnover 15-20%/yr; capital is reallocated daily toward pods with higher rolling Sharpe. Published evidence that these cuts improve returns is thin: the platforms' performance argument is selection (cut losers fast, compound winners), not a per-pod improvement.
base_rates.number: Cut 50% at -5%, terminate at -7.5% (Millennium, reported 2023); working line 2.5-3%; gross 4-8x per pod; platform vol 8-15%; PM turnover 15-20%/yr; 10-yr multi-manager composite 7.38%/yr at ~half traditional HF vol (34 firms).
base_rates.source: hedgefundinterview.com 'Pod Shop Risk Limits' citing Net Interest (Sep 2023); youngandcalculated substack 'How Multi-Manager Hedge Funds Actually Work' (2024-2025); navnoorbawa substack on Millennium (2025); longangle.com multi-strategy overview
base_rates.applicability: Pod rules exist to solve the platform's problem, which this book does not have: the allocator cannot see inside the PM's edge, so it uses realized drawdown as the only Bayesian signal of a broken model and accepts the growth cost. A single operator who can see each strategy's signal-level evidence has strictly better information than 'the pod is down 5%'. The transferable pieces are (a) capital scaled to rolling per-strategy Sharpe (the same direction as Kelly's f_i = mu_i/sigma_i^2), (b) a hard-coded review trigger rather than a sizing trigger at a drawdown level, and (c) explicit termination criteria per strategy. What should NOT transfer is the 5%/7.5% step cut: at pod vol of ~5-10% a 5% loss is a 0.5-1 sigma event, so the rule is a variance limit dressed as a risk limit.

base_rates.claim: Evidence that drawdown-based selection is informative but mostly via survivorship: hedge funds that survive prolonged large drawdowns go on to deliver outstanding performance (Darwinian selection), while low-drawdown funds are on average weak and worst in turmoil (insurance sellers); Chinese funds with contractual stop-loss termination clauses (14% of funds) have better future performance, attributed to prompt termination of bad funds, and become more risk-averse near the threshold.
base_rates.number: Drawdown-status decile analysis: large-drawdown survivors outperform, low-drawdown funds underperform and do worst in stress (Cukurova & Marin 2011); 14% of Chinese HFs carry SLCs; SLC funds show superior future performance (Pacific-Basin Finance Journal 2022).
base_rates.source: Cukurova & Marin, 'On the Economics of Hedge Fund Drawdown Status', IMDEA working paper 2011-04 (2011); 'Stop-loss early termination clause and hedge fund performance', Pacific-Basin Finance Journal 75 (2022)
base_rates.applicability: Neither paper shows that CUTTING SIZE after a drawdown improves the same strategy's subsequent returns; both show the benefit is selection across managers. Also, contrarian evidence on CTAs (buying a program mid 3-month drawdown has historically had an edge; 1,393 occurrences across 32 CTAs) points the other way for mean-reverting P&L. For a 15-strategy book the honest translation is per-strategy retire/keep decisions on pre-registered evidence (which the repo already does), not a book-wide cut.

base_rates.claim: Multi-strategy Kelly: with covariance matrix Sigma and excess-return vector mu, the growth-optimal vector is f = Sigma^-1 mu; under independence f_i = mu_i/sigma_i^2, so each strategy's risk share scales with its own Sharpe divided by its vol, and the book's Sharpe grows with the number of independent bets (Grinold: IR = IC x sqrt(breadth)). Low-correlation strategies deserve weight beyond their standalone Sharpe.
base_rates.number: f = Sigma^-1 mu; f_i = mu_i/sigma_i^2 if uncorrelated; IR = IC x sqrt(BR). Thorp's 3-asset example: optimal policy used leverage plus concentration; Frontiers (2020) study: rolling 24-month Kelly CAGR 15.0% vs tangent 10.6%, but 'about 100 trades are too few for the criterion to work properly'.
base_rates.source: Thorp (2006) Sec. 8; Grinold, 'The Fundamental Law of Active Management' (1989); Carta & Conversano, Frontiers in Applied Mathematics and Statistics (2020)
base_rates.applicability: Across the 15 strategies the growth-optimal allocation is proportional to per-strategy expected R per unit variance, adjusted for correlation (dip-buy FAMILY4 members are highly correlated with each other and with OLV on selloff days; OVS/3x fades are the natural diversifiers). Within a strategy, sizing by ex-ante conditional expectancy (e.g. OLV leg-1 avgR +0.56-0.82 vs +1.1-1.4 for leg-3+) is exactly the Kelly prescription; the repo's recency ladder is currently inverted relative to it by explicit appetite choice. Seasonal or signal-flow conditioning is legitimate under Kelly only where conditional mu/sigma^2 is estimable with more than ~100 trades per cell.

base_rates.claim: Simulated medium-term Kelly outcomes are extremely skewed and 'when in doubt bet less' is borne out: at 1.57x Kelly over 40 periods the minimum final wealth was a loss of ~10,000x initial wealth, at 1.05x Kelly 30 of 3,000 paths lost money; at 0.26x Kelly no path lost money but only 1,698/3,000 reached 10x versus 2,112 at 1.05x.
base_rates.source: Ziemba, 'Using the Kelly Criterion for Investing', Table 1.3 (Springer 2011), summarizing MacLean, Thorp, Zhao & Ziemba (2011)
base_rates.applicability: The growth-vs-security frontier is flat between ~0.5 and ~0.8 Kelly on the median (2,276 vs 2,273 paths reaching 10x) while the tail deteriorates sharply above 0.8. That supports a target band of 25-50% of HONEST Kelly for this book and says nothing is gained above ~0.8 of honest Kelly even with drawdown tolerance.

implications_for_this_book: Reframe the question from 'what fraction of backtest Kelly' to 'what fraction of honest Kelly'. Base rates put live Sharpe at 25-50% of backtest (Suhonen -73% median; McLean-Pontiff -58%; Harvey-Liu 50% rule; OFF~2). With backtest Sharpe ~2, honest Sharpe is ~0.5-1.0. The book's 6% of backtest Kelly is then 12-24% of honest Kelly, i.e. below the quarter-Kelly floor that Thorp/Benter/Ziemba practice implies, even after the harshest published haircut.

The arithmetic under GBM: current sizing is ~12% annualized vol and ~11.6% of max growth (c(2-c) at c=0.06), matching the repo's own GRM replay (Sharpe 1.85, ~21%/yr flat, maxDD -12.6%). Growth is nearly linear in size at this level: 2x size ~ 1.9x growth, 4x size ~ 3.6x growth, with vol 24%/48% and GBM lifetime P(-20% drawdown) rising from 0.07% to 3% and 19% (at honest Sharpe 1.0 the corresponding true Kelly fractions are 0.12/0.24/0.48).

A defensible target band from outside evidence is 25-50% of honest Kelly = roughly 12-25% of backtest Kelly = 2x-4x current size (vol ~24-48%). Above ~0.8 of honest Kelly the median-outcome frontier is flat and the tail deteriorates (Ziemba Table 1.3), so there is no case for going past ~50% of backtest Kelly even without a drawdown constraint.

Do the scale-up per strategy, not with one GRM: Busseti-Ryu-Boyd show uniform fractional Kelly is dominated by cutting the worst tail-per-growth bets and keeping bounded-downside bets near full size. Bounded-downside strategies (stopped dip-buys, 2-ATR-target OVS with scale-out, T+2 gap fades with demanding entries) can carry a higher Kelly fraction than no-stop stacks (OLV, Monthly Weak Close, St OS Sznl) whose GBM drawdown math does not apply.

Allocate across strategies by f_i ~ mu_i / sigma_i^2 adjusted for correlation, with a per-strategy shrinkage alpha = t^2/(t^2+1) on the strategy's own evidence (Baker-McHale form): strategies with t~2 get ~0.8 of their Kelly share, pilots with t~1.4 get ~0.66. This formalizes the pilot-tier discount already used and pushes weight toward diversifiers (OVS, 3x fades) relative to the correlated dip-buy family.

Within a strategy, Kelly says size by conditional expectancy: legs and cells with higher ex-ante avgR per unit risk (OLV leg-3+, decisive-gap OVS P1, non-midterm OVS) deserve more, not less. The OLV recency ladder and OVS cycle tilt are consistent with this direction only where they cut low-expectancy cells; the ladder as currently shipped is an appetite inversion of Kelly and should be scored as such.

Fat-tail overlay replaces the drawdown constraint: the x^(2/c-1) and RCK numbers exclude jumps (1987 -23% day; 2x leverage -> 2.85x before rebalance). If size goes to 2-4x, cap gross notional per name and per strategy (the 50% NAV OLV ticker cap becomes binding), model gap-through stop fills (already done, -45.7R book-wide), and treat the OLV book-level cap question as a jump-risk control rather than a drawdown control.

Vol targeting at the strategy-P&L level should not be expected to raise Sharpe (Cederburg 2020 real-time result; the repo's own PIT t=-0.23 throttle). Asset-level ATR sizing already captures most of the Harvey et al. tail benefit. Reserve regime conditioning for signals with an evidenced regime-dependent edge (FAMILY4 at dial >= 50), which is what the literature actually supports (momentum/BAB-style crash regimes).

Drawdown-triggered book cuts (the Millennium 5%/7.5% template) are a stop-loss on the P&L series and help only if book P&L is positively autocorrelated (Kaminski-Lo 2014). Test the ACF/regime persistence of the 23-year daily flat-basis P&L first; if losses cluster then mean-revert (typical of dip-buy books), a cut is expected to cost growth. The transferable pod-shop pieces are per-strategy rolling-Sharpe-scaled capital and explicit review/termination triggers, not step cuts.

Signal-flow and seasonality conditioning is Kelly-legitimate only where the conditional cell holds >~100 trades (Frontiers 2020: 100 trades is too few for Kelly to work properly; the repo's own MinTRL-style logic). Per-strategy cells like 'OVS midterm year' (6 years) meet the bar for a shrunk tilt (0.75x is a shrunk-Kelly number), most month-of-year cells do not.

Practical margin constraint is not binding at 2-4x: IBKR portfolio margin allows ~6.67x on stock; the book's gross at current size is a small fraction of that. The binding constraints at larger size are per-strategy daily risk caps (250 bps), ADV participation, and the concurrent-notional blindness of the T+3 fill window (up to 3 days of unfilled full-size OLV limits), all of which scale with size and should be re-derived, not left fixed, if GRM moves.
contested_points: How much to deflate the backtest Sharpe: 50% rule of thumb (Harvey-Liu 2015) vs median 73% live decay for bank alt-beta strategies (Suhonen 2017) vs 26-58% for published anomalies (McLean-Pontiff 2016). This book has mitigants (23 years, ~4,700 trades, pre-registration, a live track) that none of those samples had, so the right haircut is arguably at the mild end; the difference between honest Sharpe 0.5 and 1.0 is a 2x difference in every recommended size.

Whether fractional Kelly should be set by estimation error (Thorp fig. 5, Baker-McHale) or by drawdown tolerance (Thorp's 'psychological comfort of half Kelly'). The principal has removed the second motive, which under the first motive alone still lands at 25-50% of honest Kelly, not at full Kelly.

Thorp's own fraction is reported as quarter Kelly by some secondary sources and half Kelly by others; his primary text recommends 'half Kelly or some nearby value'. Ziemba's claim that Buffett behaves like a full-Kelly (no-borrowing) investor and Keynes like an 80% Kelly investor is an inference from concentration, not a stated policy.

Vol targeting: Moreira-Muir (2017) and Barroso-Santa-Clara (2015) show large in-sample Sharpe gains; Cederburg et al. (2020) show implementable real-time versions across 103 strategies generally underperform; Harvey et al. (2018) find gains only for equities/credit. The disagreement is about implementability, not about the in-sample fact.

Drawdown cuts: Kaminski-Lo (2014) make the benefit conditional on positive autocorrelation; Cukurova-Marin (2011) find large-drawdown SURVIVORS outperform (i.e. cutting them would have been wrong) while the 2022 Chinese SLC study finds funds with termination clauses do better via prompt termination. All three are about selection across managers; none isolates the effect of cutting size on the same strategy's forward return.

Whether uniform fractional Kelly (what GRM implements) is an acceptable approximation to risk-constrained Kelly. Busseti-Ryu-Boyd (2016) show ~34% higher growth at equal drawdown risk from heterogeneous bets, but their examples are stylized; Klass-Nowicki (2005) show the Grossman-Zhou continuous solution is not optimal in discrete time.

GBM drawdown probabilities (x^(2/c-1)) vs jump risk: Thorp himself flags 1987 as the reason not to trust the continuous math at leverage >= 2x; the disagreement is how much of the book's tail is jump-driven (OLV no-stop stacks, gap-through shorts) versus diffusive.

Pod-shop numbers are journalist/insider reporting, not audited: Millennium 5%/7.5% is widely repeated but unpublished by the firm; per-pod vol targets and gross leverage are ranges, and no public study shows the cut rules improve pod-level returns rather than platform selection.

outside_evidence.topic: Calendar seasonality relevant to a 1-63 day US equity book: turn-of-month, opex week, day-of-week, Sep/Oct, Halloween, January/small-cap, pre-holiday, earnings-season effects on reversal/momentum, and post-publication persistence of each

base_rates.claim: Classic turn-of-the-month (TOM): days -1..+3 carried ALL of the DJIA's positive return over 90 years; ~12 bp/day on TOM days vs ~0 elsewhere
base_rates.number: DJIA 1897-1986: 4-day window [-1,+3] = 100% of cumulative gain; ~0.12%/day. McConnell & Xu extension: CRSP 1987-2005, again all excess market return inside the 4-day window
base_rates.source: Lakonishok & Smidt, RFS 1988; Xu & McConnell 2008 (Purdue working paper / FAJ)
base_rates.applicability: NEEDS IN-REPO CONFIRMATION for the current decade. The 1897-2005 base rate is strong, but see the next two rows: the [0,+3] window has decayed to insignificance in US large-cap since ~2015. Treat the 4-day window as a weak long-side prior (maybe +5-10 bp/day), not a sizing input on its own.

base_rates.claim: TOM decay in the ETF era: the classical [0,+3] window is now indistinguishable from other days in SPY/QQQ/IWM; a wider [-3,+3] window still shows +5 to +12 bp/day but with a consistent downtrend over the last decade, steepest post-2015; QQQ's early-2000s TOM effect decayed to zero; what remains is concentrated on the FIRST trading day and in equal-weighted (small-cap) baskets
base_rates.number: [-3,+3] window: +5-12 bp/day above other days for US ETFs, EWZ +23 bp; [0,+3] window: no significant difference in US equities; TOM-only switching strategy underperforms buy-and-hold in SPY/QQQ/IWM on CAGR and Sharpe (5 bp costs)
base_rates.source: QuantSeeker 'Turn-of-the-Month Strategies: Do They Still Work?' (rolling analysis incl. Chen et al 2015 [1996-2012], McGroarty et al 2019 [1961-2015]); FPA Journal 2011 'TOM anomaly in the age of ETFs' (effect concentrated on first trading day post-ETF)
base_rates.applicability: Size-relevant only as a small tilt: a long-bias dip-buy entered on T-8..T-4 selling-pressure days and exiting into T-3..T+3 aligns with the surviving mechanism; do not carry a standalone TOM long. Equal-weight persistence means the overflow tier (small/mid) is where any residual lives, and that tier's ledger is survivorship-flattered (CLAUDE.md caveat).

base_rates.claim: 'Dash for cash' (Etula, Rinne, Suominen, Vaittinen): institutional month-end cash needs produce selling pressure T-8..T-4 and a reversal T-3..T+3, anchored to the LAST SETTLEMENT DAY before month end (T-3 under T+3 settlement); stronger in large, liquid, mutual-fund-held stocks; stronger over time in the US as fund ownership rose
base_rates.number: Post-1995 (T+3 settlement): CRSP VW avg -17 bp over T-8..T-4 vs +77 bp over T-3..T+3; S&P 500 annualized -3.4% (T-8..T-4) vs +28.6% (T-3..start of next month); found across global indices
base_rates.source: Etula, Rinne, Suominen & Vaittinen, 'Dash for Cash: Monthly Market Impact of Institutional Liquidity Needs', RFS 33(1):75-111
base_rates.applicability: CREDIBLE PRIOR with one live caveat: US settlement moved to T+1 on 2024-05-28, so the settlement-anchored day is now T-1, not T-3. The mechanism (cash-need selling then reversal) should survive but its calendar position shifts and the prior decay (QuantSeeker) may partly BE this shift. Confirm in repo on post-2024 data before anchoring anything to T-3. Best use: a mild bias toward FULL size for liquid-tier dip-buys signalled T-8..T-4 (they enter into the pressure) and a mild bias against new short entries (OVS, 3x fades) with holds that span T-3..T+3.

base_rates.claim: Option-expiration week (Stivers & Sun): large-cap optionable stocks earn most of their weekly return in the third-Friday week, with a small giveback the following week; no effect before listed options existed
base_rates.number: 28 S&P 100 names, 1996-2008: opex week +0.45% vs +0.12% other weeks; weekly Sharpe 0.57 vs 0.07; high option/stock-volume subset (7.5% of weeks) +0.83% (Sharpe 1.25); week AFTER opex -0.03% vs +0.18% for other non-opex weeks; 1948-1972 (pre-options) third-Friday week not unusual
base_rates.source: Stivers & Sun, 'Returns and option activity over the option-expiration week for S&P 100 stocks', J. Banking & Finance 37(11):4226-4240; CXO Advisory drill-down
base_rates.applicability: CREDIBLE PRIOR (mechanism = delta-hedge unwinds + falling IV into expiry; structural, not sentiment) but small: +33 bp/week on the index, and a 2025 SPY re-test says it has deteriorated in the last four years. Use as a tie-breaker for long-side sizing in opex week and a mild haircut on short entries (OVS, 3x fades) opened Mon-Wed of opex week; nothing more.

base_rates.claim: SPY opex-week re-test 1993-2025: opex week is positive on average but weak, month-dependent, and fading
base_rates.number: Buy opex-week open / sell Friday close: +0.2% avg per week, 2% CAGR at ~18% time in market; July and January opex weeks net negative, April strongest; opex DAY itself compounds to -23.6% (51.4% win, avg win +0.60% / avg loss -0.77%); 'deteriorated over the last four years'
base_rates.source: QuantifiedStrategies.com / Substack, 'The Options Expiration Week Effect' (SPY 1993-2025)
base_rates.applicability: Supports treating opex week as a +0.2%/week tilt with no January/July effect. The week-after-opex-in-September stat (avg -0.94%, 25% win) is the same cell the repo's T3 SEP_POSTQUAD_SHORT already trades; do not double count it.

base_rates.claim: Monday/day-of-week effect is dead for large-cap indices since the 1990s; what survives is cross-sectional (speculative stocks weak Monday/strong Friday) and conditional (Turnaround Tuesday after a bad Monday)
base_rates.number: US/UK/Germany: Monday effect present 1970s-80s, vanished 1990s-2000s (Kohers et al 2004; Steeley 2001). CXO SPY 1993-2017 (6,188 days): Tuesday relatively strong, Thu/Fri weak, Monday-overnight advantage failed in the most recent subperiod. Birru JFE 2018: Monday accounts for >100% of long-short returns for anomalies whose SHORT leg is the speculative leg; speculative stocks lower Monday, higher Friday
base_rates.source: Kohers, Kohers, Pandey & Kohers 2004; CXO Advisory 'SPY by Day of the Week and Overnight' 2017; Birru, 'Day of the week and the cross-section of returns', JFE 130(1):182-214
base_rates.applicability: IGNORE the generic Monday-negative prior for index sizing. CREDIBLE PRIOR for the cross-section: shorts of speculative/high-vol names (OVS, 3x-ETF fades) have their best expected day on Monday and worst on Friday; long dip-buys in speculative names should not be sized up for a Friday entry. Monday Dip / SPY-QQQ MonFri Reversion are consistent with the surviving conditional effect (next row).

base_rates.claim: Turnaround Tuesday: after a sharply down Monday, Tuesday is strongly positive since 2010
base_rates.number: S&P 500 since 2010: after Monday <= -1.5%, Tuesday avg +0.9%, ~70% positive, vs ordinary Tuesday +0.1% / 54%; after Monday <= -2%, next day avg +1.2%; after Thu+Fri+Mon(>=2%) down: +1.6%, 21 of 31 positive; Tuesday vol roughly doubles in those cases (avg up +1.86%, avg down -1.43%)
base_rates.source: Sherwood News / Bespoke, CNBC (Feb 2020), QuantifiedStrategies 'Turnaround Tuesday' backtest
base_rates.applicability: CREDIBLE PRIOR supporting the Monday-dip family's existence; it is the same edge the book already backtests so it is confirmation, not an extra tilt. Note the doubling of conditional vol: an ATR-sized position already shrinks on these days, so do not add a calendar boost on top of what the vol-scaling gives.

base_rates.claim: September is the only month with a negative long-run S&P 500 average and a sub-50% hit rate; the average is real but statistically fragile and driven by a handful of years
base_rates.number: S&P 500 since 1950: Sept avg -0.6%, 34 up / 41 down (45%); since 1980: -0.9%; since 2000: -1.4% (13/13); 1928-2025: -1.13%; NASDAQ since 2000: -1.9%. February is the only other negative month (-0.03%). Rough significance (own calc, sd ~4.5%/month, N=75): t ~ -1.1 vs zero, ~ -2.3 vs the +0.7% all-month mean; the >10% plunges are 1974 and 2002 (Sept), 1987 and 2008 (Oct)
base_rates.source: Motley Fool 'September effect statistics'; Macrobond 'Villain of Wall Street' (1928-2025); Verdence; own t calc
base_rates.applicability: NEEDS IN-REPO CONFIRMATION per strategy. As a direction prior it is worth maybe 0.9x on new long-side sizing in September, not a stand-down; the cell is dominated by 2001/2002/2008/2011/2022 which are also high-fragility-dial months, so the repo's dial machinery already captures most of it. Do not stack a calendar cut on top of a dial cut.

base_rates.claim: Midterm-year September/October are weaker than average, and the midterm-year autumn low to year-end rally is larger than in other years
base_rates.number: Last 10 midterm Septembers: negative 6 of 10, avg about -2%; midterm Octobers avg about -3% (Hirsch/Gue, small N); 1950-2022 midterm years: avg intra-year drawdown -18%; autumn-low-to-year-end +13.6% mean / +12.0% median in midterm years vs +9.1% non-midterm; midterm years positive ~87% with strong 12-month-after-midterm returns
base_rates.source: Stock Trader's Almanac (Hirsch), Elliott Gue Substack, Chase, IBKR Campus, simianx.ai (1950-2026)
base_rates.applicability: NEEDS IN-REPO CONFIRMATION (N=19 midterm years, cells of 10). The repo already runs OVS at 0.75x in midterm years on its own evidence. A tentative extension: long-side dip-buys sized up into Q4 of a midterm year after an autumn low, short-side (OVS/3x fades) at full size Aug-Oct. Treat as a 10-20% tilt at most.

base_rates.claim: Realized volatility is seasonal: highest Aug-Oct (October the max), lowest mid-summer; VIX median climbs into October
base_rates.number: October has hosted the most >1%, >2%, >3%, >5%, >7% and >10% daily moves since 1930; avg absolute monthly change Oct 1987-Oct 2016: Oct 4.3%, Sept 3.9%, Nov 3.8%; VIX median since 1990: ~16.5 late Aug -> ~18 mid-Sept -> ~19 early Oct (VIX +4.4% avg in October); October avg price return still +1.4% over the last 35 years
base_rates.source: Barchart 'Is October the most volatile month'; Yahoo Finance Chart of the Day (VIX seasonal medians); Jeff Hirsch; StoneX seasonality
base_rates.applicability: CREDIBLE PRIOR but ALREADY PRICED into ATR-based sizing: share counts fall automatically as ATR rises. The sizing question is whether R-per-trade edge changes with the season, not whether vol does. For the dip-buy/reversal families the Nagel evidence (below) says the edge RISES with vol, so seasonal vol is not a reason to cut risk bps in autumn.

base_rates.claim: Halloween/Sell-in-May: Nov-Apr beats May-Oct globally over very long samples and held out of sample in all 37 original markets, but on the S&P 500 it is not significant in the modern era, is driven by outliers, and mostly lives in small caps
base_rates.number: Jacobsen & Zhang: 114 markets, 37,167 monthly obs; total risk premium ~4%, ALL earned Nov-Apr; summer returns 1.1% BELOW the risk-free rate; winter-summer gap 4.52% (6.25% last 50 yrs); OOS positive in all 37 Bouman-Jacobsen 2002 markets. US 1950-2025: Nov-Apr 7.0% annualized vs May-Oct 2.1%; buy-and-hold CAGR 8.05% vs sell-in-May 6.86%. Dec 1983-Dec 2009: effect NOT significant for S&P 500, significant for Russell 2000. Dichtl & Drobetz 2015: strongly weakened or disappeared post-publication, driven by extreme monthly observations. Hong & Yu 2009: summer VW return lower by 0.90%/month (t=2.42), turnover lower, spreads wider, 51 markets
base_rates.source: Bouman & Jacobsen AER 2002; Jacobsen & Zhang J. Int'l Money & Finance 2020 (SSRN 2154873); Lambda Finance SPY backtest 1950-2025; American J. Finance & Accounting 2014 (S&P vs Russell); Dichtl & Drobetz IRFA 2015; Hong & Yu JFM 2009
base_rates.applicability: NEEDS IN-REPO CONFIRMATION. For a liquid large-cap book the summer half is 'lower drift, lower liquidity', which cuts two ways: lower liquidity is a headwind for breakouts (52wh, Sector BO) and a tailwind for liquidity-provision reversals (OLV, dip-buys) per Nagel. The right in-repo test is per-family avgR by half-year, not the index drift. Do NOT size the whole book down in summer on this evidence.

base_rates.claim: January effect: small-cap January premium was concentrated in the first five trading days, has trended down since 1988 for both large and small indices, and is now judged untradeable after costs; the year-end tax-loss mechanism still shows up in reversal and momentum strategies
base_rates.number: Keim 1983: >50% of the January size premium in the first 5 trading days, much of it on day 1. Gu 2003: pronounced declining trend since 1988 in both Russell size indices. Quantpedia (1947-2007): 12.7%/yr with -55% max DD, 'becoming impossible to trade'. George & Hwang 2004: 52-week-high momentum +0.45%/month all months vs +1.23%/month ex-January (implies roughly -8% in January). Short-term reversal: +2.4% to +2.7% risk-adjusted in January alone (Hameed et al)
base_rates.source: Keim JFE 1983; Gu, 'The declining January effect', Q. Rev. Econ. & Finance 2003; Haug & Hirschey FAJ 2006; Quantpedia; George & Hwang JF 2004; Hameed, Huang & Mian 'Industries and stock return reversals'
base_rates.applicability: IGNORE the small-cap January long as a sizing input (costs, decline, survivorship in the overflow tier). CREDIBLE PRIOR that January is the worst month for nearness-to-52-week-high momentum: the 52wh Breakout and Sector BO strategies deserve an in-repo January check with a prior of ~0.5-0.75x; reversal families (OLV, dip-buys) get a mild January tailwind.

base_rates.claim: Same-calendar-month return seasonality in the cross-section persists for up to 20 years and survived out of sample internationally
base_rates.number: Heston & Sadka JFE 2008: same-month relative performance predicts at lags 12, 24, ... up to 20 years, independent of size, industry, earnings dates. Keloharju, Linnainmaa & Nyberg JF 2016: strategy on historical same-month returns earns ~13%/yr. German OOS 1998-2017: long-short raw returns up to 233 bp/month
base_rates.source: Heston & Sadka JFE 2008; Keloharju, Linnainmaa & Nyberg, 'Return Seasonalities', JF 71(4):1557-1590; EFMA 2017 German out-of-sample study
base_rates.applicability: CREDIBLE PRIOR that ticker-month seasonal ranks carry information, which underwrites the book's seasonal-rank strategies (St OS Sznl, Weak Close Decent Sznls, Seasonal Rank Divergence signal). The effect is a monthly-horizon cross-sectional spread, ~1%/month; it says the seasonal filter is not noise, not that a specific 5-day cell is reliable. In-repo confirmation on the repo's own rank definitions is still required (the memory note says famous calendar cells on liquid names were arbitraged post-2013).

base_rates.claim: Pre-holiday effect (Ariel) is gone for large-cap indices and survives only in small firms
base_rates.number: 1963-1982: pre-holiday days returned 9-14x the mean of other days; 8 pre-holiday days/yr = >1/3 of total market return. 1983-2019: pre-holiday vs other-day difference t = 0.64 (DJIA), 0.93 (S&P 500); effect only among small firms. Santa Claus window (last 5 + first 2 sessions) since 1950: +1.3% avg, 79% positive vs +0.3% / 58% for a random 7-day window
base_rates.source: Ariel JF 1990; Ko, 'The Pre-Holiday Premium of Ariel (1990) Has Largely Become a Small-Firm Effect Out of Sample', Critical Finance Review 2021; LPL Research (Santa rally)
base_rates.applicability: IGNORE for the liquid tier. The Santa window is one 7-day observation per year and should not enter sizing; the overflow tier may retain a small-firm pre-holiday tailwind but the repo's overflow ledger cannot confirm it cleanly.

base_rates.claim: Short-term reversal is ~6x larger around earnings announcements (compensation for market-maker inventory risk), and the earnings-driven component of returns does NOT reverse (it drifts)
base_rates.number: So & Wang JFE 2014, 1996-2011: 3-day reversal-strategy return +1.45% around earnings announcements vs +0.22% in pseudo-announcement windows. Chan, Jegadeesh & Lakonishok JF 1996: earnings-surprise momentum and price momentum are separate, both drift, little subsequent reversal. Da, Liu & Schaumburg (NY Fed SR 513): reversal profits positive and significant in 1982-89, 1990-99, 2000-09 but declining over time; the earnings-announcement component shows no reversal
base_rates.source: So & Wang, 'News-driven return reversals: Liquidity provision ahead of earnings announcements', JFE 2014; Chan, Jegadeesh & Lakonishok JF 1996; Da, Liu & Schaumburg, 'Decomposing short-term return reversal', FRBNY 2011
base_rates.applicability: Two-sided. The book blacks out OVS +-10 td around earnings and cuts OLV/St OS Sznl sizes pre-print on its own ledger evidence (St OS -0.50 avgR straddling prints). The outside evidence says pre-announcement reversal is REAL but is paid for with jump risk, i.e. the mean is positive and the tail is fat; the repo's finding that the tail dominated its small sample is consistent. Keep the blackout/overrides; the outside prior does not justify relaxing them for a no-stop 5-10 day holder.

base_rates.claim: Momentum profits are quarterly seasonal: ~5x higher in quarter-end months (window dressing + tax-loss selling), strongest in December and in high-institutional-ownership names
base_rates.number: US, ex-January: momentum +310 bp/month in quarter-ending months (Mar/Jun/Sep/Dec) vs +59 bp in other months
base_rates.source: Sias, 'Causes and Seasonality of Momentum Profits', FAJ 63(2):48-54
base_rates.applicability: NEEDS IN-REPO CONFIRMATION for 52wh Breakout / Sector BO: a prior that breakout follow-through is better in Mar/Jun/Sep/Dec (and worst in January). Cheap to test on the ledger's ~signal-month buckets; size by no more than 1.25x in quarter-end months if it confirms.

base_rates.claim: Expected returns to short-term reversal (liquidity provision) rise sharply with VIX; even industry-portfolio reversals become high-Sharpe in high-VIX periods
base_rates.number: Nagel RFS 2012: reversal-strategy expected return and conditional Sharpe 'increase enormously' with VIX; 2007-09 the peak; predictable ex ante from VIX level
base_rates.source: Nagel, 'Evaporating Liquidity', RFS 25(7):2005-2039
base_rates.applicability: CREDIBLE PRIOR and the single most sizing-relevant outside result for this book: the dip-buy / OLV / Monday-dip families are liquidity provision, and the outside base rate says their edge per unit of risk RISES in high-vol regimes. This conflicts on its face with the repo's FAMILY4 0.25x band at dial >= 50 (clustered t = -1.96, p = 0.057 on PIT weights). Reconciliation to test in repo: the fragility composite is not VIX; condition FAMILY4 avgR on VIX-level terciles and on dial separately. If VIX-high/dial-low cells are strong, the band is cutting the wrong thing.

base_rates.claim: Momentum crashes are forecastable: they follow market declines, occur when market vol is high, and coincide with sharp rebounds; loser-decile betas exceed 3
base_rates.number: 1927-2013 sample; momentum strategy lost about -45.6% over Mar-Apr 2009; past-loser beta > 3 and past-winner beta < 0.5 after major declines; vol-scaled dynamic momentum roughly doubles alpha and Sharpe
base_rates.source: Daniel & Moskowitz, 'Momentum Crashes', JFE 122(2):221-247
