base_rates.applicability: CREDIBLE PRIOR for the long-breakout and 3x-fade legs: after a >15-20% drawdown with high vol, breakout longs (52wh, Sector BO, ATR Ext) are the wrong side of a rebound and short-side fades of beaten-down names (3x Bear fade) are the right side. The repo's 3x Leader Gap Fade / 3x Bear Fade already live here; the outside evidence supports NOT frag-banding the leader fade (as the repo decided) and supports vol-scaling breakouts.

base_rates.claim: Pre-FOMC announcement drift: large through 2011, essentially gone since 2015
base_rates.number: Sept 1994-Mar 2011: +49 bp in the 24h before scheduled FOMC statements, ~80% of annual excess return; post-2015: drift 'essentially disappeared' in both press-conference and non-press-conference meetings
base_rates.source: Lucca & Moench JF 2015; Boguth, Gregoire & Martineau 2019; 'The disappearing pre-FOMC announcement drift', Finance Research Letters 2020
base_rates.applicability: IGNORE as a sizing input beyond what the repo's event sleeve (T1/T2) already pre-registered; the repo's Pre-FOMC Rally fragility signal is a risk flag, not a return prior. Any new FOMC-anchored tilt needs post-2015 evidence only.

base_rates.claim: Post-publication decay base rate: cross-sectional predictors lose about a quarter of their return out of sample and over half after publication; the decline is US-specific and larger for higher in-sample returns and for liquid, low-idiosyncratic-risk stocks; anomaly profits roughly halved after 2001 decimalization and DAILY-horizon anomaly profits essentially vanished in the early 2000s
base_rates.number: McLean & Pontiff: 97 predictors, -26% out of sample, -58% post-publication (-32% attributable to publication). Jacobs & Müller: 241 anomalies, 39 markets, US the only country with a reliable post-publication decline. Chordia, Subrahmanyam & Tong: anomaly portfolio returns ~halved post-decimalization; daily anomaly profits vanished since early 2000s
base_rates.source: McLean & Pontiff JF 2016; Jacobs & Müller JFE 135(1):213-230 2020; Chordia, Subrahmanyam & Tong JAE 2014
base_rates.applicability: CREDIBLE PRIOR for haircutting any seasonal cell the repo discovers in-sample: apply ~0.5-0.75x to the in-sample edge before sizing on it; calendar cells on liquid large caps are exactly the category (public, cheap to arbitrage) that decays most. The book's backtest Sharpe ~2 at ~6% of full Kelly already embeds a large decay haircut; that is roughly consistent with a 50% edge haircut plus estimation-error shrinkage.

implications_for_this_book: Rank of outside evidence for sizing use: (1) Nagel 2012 vol-conditioned reversal edge is the one result strong enough to change a rule: dip-buy / OLV / Monday-dip families are liquidity provision whose expected return per unit risk rises with VIX. The FAMILY4 0.25x band at dial >= 50 is in tension with it. Run a repo test that conditions FAMILY4 and OLV avgR on VIX-level terciles and on the dial separately; if the damage lives in dial-high/VIX-low cells (distribution/leadership deterioration without a vol spike) the band is fine, if it lives in VIX-high cells the band is fighting the strongest documented edge in the class.

Credible-prior cells (size with a modest tilt, no in-repo confirmation needed for direction, confirm magnitude): month-end selling pressure T-8..T-4 then reversal into T+3 (large liquid names, fund-held) after re-anchoring to T+1 settlement; opex-week long tilt of ~+20-45 bp/week on optionable large caps with a small giveback the week after; Monday-weak/Friday-strong in speculative names (shorts of high-vol names best entered for Monday, dip-buys of speculative names not boosted on Friday entries); January weak for nearness-to-52-week-high momentum (prior ~0.5-0.75x on 52wh Breakout / Sector BO in January); post-decline high-vol regimes are momentum-crash regimes (do not vol-boost breakouts there, do keep the 3x leader/bear fades exempt from frag cuts as the repo already does).

Needs-in-repo-confirmation cells (direction plausible, magnitude and current existence uncertain): September (-0.6% avg since 1950, 45% hit, t ~ -1 vs zero, driven by ~5 years that also carried high fragility readings, so a calendar cut would double count the dial); midterm-year Aug-Oct weakness and Q4 rally (N=19); Halloween for large caps (not significant 1984-2009; summer is lower-liquidity per Hong-Yu, which should HELP reversal strategies and HURT breakouts: test per family, not on index drift); quarter-end-month momentum (Sias +310 vs +59 bp/month) as a 1.25x prior on breakout strategies in Mar/Jun/Sep/Dec; ticker-month seasonal ranks (Heston-Sadka / Keloharju) on the repo's own rank definitions.

Ignore cells (do not size on them): generic Monday-negative index effect (dead since the 1990s); pre-holiday premium on large caps (t 0.64-0.93 since 1983); small-cap January long (declining since 1988, untradeable after costs, overflow-tier survivorship); pre-FOMC drift (gone since 2015); Santa Claus rally (one 7-day obs/yr); classic [0,+3] TOM long in SPY/QQQ (insignificant last decade).

Seasonal vol is already in the sizing: Aug-Oct realized vol is the highest of the year and October has the most >1/2/3% days since 1930, but ATR-based share sizing shrinks positions automatically. A calendar cut on top of ATR sizing in autumn would be a double cut. The relevant question for each family is whether R-per-trade changes with season, which is a per-strategy ledger bucket test the orchestrator can run cheaply (signal month x family avgR with episode clustering).

Earnings seasons: outside evidence says pre-announcement reversal is ~6x normal but is compensation for jump risk, and the earnings-news component of returns drifts rather than reverses. That supports the repo's existing blackouts and pre-print size overrides for no-stop holders (OVS blackout, OLV/St OS overrides) and does not support relaxing them. It also implies the reversal families' edge outside earnings windows is smaller than the all-days average, which the repo's ledger buckets already reflect.

Haircut discipline for any new seasonal tilt: McLean-Pontiff (-26% OOS, -58% post-publication) and Chordia et al (daily anomaly profits gone since early 2000s on liquid names) say calendar cells on liquid large caps are the most decay-prone category. Any in-repo seasonal cell should be sized at 0.5-0.75x its in-sample edge, capped at +-25% of base bps, and only after an episode-clustered test; the cells above that pass 'credible prior' still only justify tilts of that size, never a stand-down or a >1.25x boost.

Structural date changes to respect: US T+1 settlement (2024-05-28) moves the Etula settlement anchor from T-3 to T-1, so any month-end window computed on pre-2024 data is misaligned by two sessions; test the 2024-2026 subsample before using it. Opex-week behaviour has deteriorated in the last four years (SPY re-test) and the week-after-opex September cell is already the repo's T3 trade, so do not add a second September post-opex short.
contested_points: Halloween/Sell-in-May: Jacobsen & Zhang (114 markets, all risk premium earned Nov-Apr, OOS positive in all 37 original markets) vs Dichtl & Drobetz 2015 (weakened or gone post-publication once implementable, driven by outlier months) and the 1984-2009 finding that it is insignificant for the S&P 500 but significant for the Russell 2000. Both sides agree the modern large-cap US effect is weak; disagreement is about whether the global pattern is a real premium or an outlier artifact.

Turn-of-the-month persistence: Lakonishok-Smidt and McConnell-Xu (1897-2005, all excess return in 4 days) vs 2019-2025 rolling re-tests (US [0,+3] window insignificant, steep decline post-2015). Unresolved whether the decay is arbitrage, the shift of flows toward the first trading day, or the 2017/2024 settlement changes moving the Etula anchor.

Vol-conditioned reversal sizing: Nagel 2012 says reversal/liquidity-provision edge rises with VIX; the repo's own PIT test says FAMILY4 dip-buys degrade at high fragility (t = -1.96, p = 0.057, small N, negative in 6 of 9 years). The two can both be true if the fragility composite captures deterioration that is distinct from VIX level; nobody has run that split in the repo.

September: the negative mean is consistent across 1928-, 1950-, 1980-, 2000- windows, but the t-statistic vs zero is ~ -1 and the effect is concentrated in a few crisis years; academic treatments call it fragile while practitioner sources call it the most reliable monthly cell. Midterm-year sub-cells have N=10.

January effect: Haug & Hirschey (2006) say the small-cap January effect is 'alive and well' and consistent, Gu (2003) and Quantpedia say it has trended down since 1988 and is untradeable net of costs; the evidence that investors arbitraged it away specifically is weak (it may have reverted to pre-1963 levels rather than been traded out).

Opex week: Stivers-Sun's +0.45% vs +0.12% (1996-2008, 28 names) has not been replicated on the same universe post-2008 in a peer-reviewed venue; the SPY 1993-2025 practitioner re-test finds a smaller +0.2%/week that has deteriorated in the last four years, and a separate practitioner series claims the 4-day opex window compounds negative. Definitions (whole week vs Friday only vs the 4 days around) drive the sign.

Day-of-week: index-level effect gone; Birru's cross-sectional Monday/Friday mood pattern (1963-2013 style samples) has not been shown to persist post-2015 out of sample, and the 'Turnaround Tuesday' numbers come from since-2010 samples with N in the low hundreds and vol that doubles on those days.

Pre-earnings reversal: So & Wang show a 6x reversal premium that a market maker earns for bearing announcement jump risk; whether a 5-10 day no-stop holder captures that premium or only the jump is exactly the question the repo's small-N St OS Sznl pre-print cell (N=9, avgR -0.50) cannot settle.

Post-publication decay magnitude: McLean-Pontiff's 58% is a US cross-sectional-anomaly average; calendar effects on indices are not in their 97 predictors, and Jacobs-Müller find no reliable decay outside the US. Applying 0.5-0.75x to an in-repo seasonal cell is a judgment, not a measured base rate for this exact category.

outside_evidence.topic: Volatility-managed portfolios, regime sizing, conditional correlation, drawdown-triggered de-risking, and reversal-by-VIX evidence, mapped to three questions: (1) dial-armed beta hedge on a short-term MR/breakout book, (2) sizing mean-reversion UP in high VIX, (3) a book-level vol target

base_rates.claim: Volatility-managed market portfolio (weight = c / prior-month realized variance) earns a large alpha vs buy-and-hold, with a beta well below 1
base_rates.number: Alpha 4.86%/yr (SE 1.56), beta 0.61, appraisal ratio 0.33, buy-and-hold Sharpe 0.42, managed Sharpe ~25% higher; momentum factor managed alpha 12.51%/yr (largest of 9 factors); 20 OECD indices: managed Sharpe +0.15 on average, higher in 80% of countries; 65% mean-variance utility gain; MPPM 75% higher
base_rates.source: Moreira & Muir, Journal of Finance 72(4), NBER w22208 (1926-2015 US)
base_rates.applicability: Supports (3) in principle for long beta exposure: E[R]/Var of the market falls when vol spikes because vol moves are not matched by expected-return moves. Direct relevance to this book is the LONG-ONLY beta carried by the dip-buy sleeves (FAMILY4, OLV), not the reversal alpha itself.

base_rates.claim: The managed-market alpha survives realistic trading costs but is eroded by them; leverage-capped versions keep less than half of it
base_rates.number: Alpha 4.86% pre-cost -> 4.77% (1 bp), 3.98% (10 bps), 3.63% (14 bps incl. cost rising with VIX 20->40); break-even cost 56 bps; no-leverage version (min(c/RV^2,1)) alpha 2.12%, 1.5x leverage cap 3.10%; average absolute monthly weight change 0.73 for the RV^2 rule
base_rates.source: Moreira & Muir Table 4
base_rates.applicability: A book-level vol target on a 1-63 day book turns over the whole notional each time vol reprices; the paper's own turnover (73% of notional per month for the pure rule) is the cost line item that Barroso-Detzel later show kills it for every factor but the market.

base_rates.claim: Real-time (expanding-window) volatility management does NOT systematically beat unmanaged portfolios across a broad anomaly set; benefits concentrate in momentum, profitability and BAB
base_rates.number: 103 equity strategies; in-sample managed Sharpe higher in roughly half to 60% (secondary summaries report 53/103 and 63/103); only 8/103 show consistently higher Sharpe; out-of-sample versions 'generally earn lower certainty equivalent returns and Sharpe ratios'; cause = structural instability of spanning regressions
base_rates.source: Cederburg, O'Doherty, Wang & Yan, JFE 138(1):95-117
base_rates.applicability: Undercuts (3): a scalar vol rule fitted on the ledger will look good in-sample and the base rate for it surviving OOS across non-momentum strategies is poor. The one family where it robustly survives is momentum/trend, i.e. this book's 52wh Breakout / Sector BO sleeves, not the dip-buys.

base_rates.claim: Per-factor OOS Sharpe with vs without volatility management (1977-2020, expanding window, gross of costs)
base_rates.number: MKT 0.530 -> 0.408; SMB 0.208 -> 0.068; HML 0.170 -> 0.194; RMW 0.506 -> 0.527; CMA 0.399 -> 0.355; UMD 0.474 -> 1.035; ROE 0.722 -> 1.094; IA 0.508 -> 0.605; BAB 0.880 -> 1.321. Net of costs with trading diversification: MKT 0.519 -> 0.433, UMD 0.114 -> 0.209, RMW 0.356 -> 0.226. Conditional MULTIfactor portfolio: OOS net-of-cost Sharpe +13% vs unconditional (p<0.01)
base_rates.source: DeMiguel, Martin-Utrera & Uppal, Journal of Finance, Table I
base_rates.applicability: Cleanest single table for (3): vol scaling the market/beta leg LOSES ~0.1 Sharpe OOS while scaling momentum roughly doubles it. Scaling the whole book with one number blends a winner (breakout sleeves) with losers (beta-carrying dip-buys); the multifactor result says do it at the sleeve-weight level, not the book level, if at all.

base_rates.claim: After transaction costs, volatility management of factors other than the market produces ~zero abnormal returns and significantly LOWER Sharpe ratios; the managed market survives only in easy-to-arbitrage stocks and only when sentiment is high
base_rates.number: 9 factors, 5 cost-mitigation variants; non-market factors: zero net alpha, Sharpe reduced; managed market: profitable net of costs, alpha concentrated in low-arbitrage-risk stocks; outperforms only in high-sentiment periods
base_rates.source: Barroso & Detzel, JFE 140(3):744-767
base_rates.applicability: Second independent undercut of (3) for anything that is not the beta leg.

base_rates.claim: Vol targeting (10% target, 60 assets 1926-2017) raises Sharpe for risk assets (equities, credit) but is negligible for bonds, FX, commodities; it thins left tails everywhere; vol-of-vol on US equities falls sharply
base_rates.number: US equity vol-of-vol 4.6% unscaled -> 1.8% scaled; Sharpe gain for equities/credit attributed to the leverage effect; 'negligible' for bonds, currencies, commodities; left-tail events less severe because they occur when exposure is already small; outperformance absent 'during the middle part of the sample'
base_rates.source: Harvey, Hoyle, Korgaonkar, Rattray, Sargaison & Van Hemert, JPM 45(1):14-33
base_rates.applicability: The mechanism (leverage effect + vol clustering) is a property of LONG equity beta. This book's ATR-unit position sizing already inverse-vol scales each position; the residual argument for a book-level target is only the beta the long sleeves net to.

base_rates.claim: Conditional vol targeting (act only when prior-month vol is in the top or bottom quintile) beats conventional continuous targeting on Sharpe, drawdown, turnover and leverage; conventional targeting can WIDEN drawdowns
base_rates.number: 10 equity markets: conventional raised Sharpe in 8/10, conditional in 10/10; conventional increased max DD in UK/Canada/Australia/Hong Kong by 4% to 34.4%; conditional cut max DD by 6.6 pts on average; momentum factors max DD 54.1% -> 20.1% and Sharpe more than doubled; annual turnover 1.4 (conditional) vs 2.1 (conventional, often >200%); leverage capped at 200% in low-vol state
base_rates.source: Bongaerts, Kang & van Dijk, Financial Analysts Journal 76(4)
base_rates.applicability: If any dial-conditioned book-level rule is adopted, the evidence favors a two-state extreme-quintile switch over a continuous scalar. Note this is in-sample design, no expanding-window test; it replicates Moreira-Muir's strongest result (momentum) and its weakest (market) exactly as Cederburg/DeMiguel would predict.

base_rates.claim: Multi-asset 60/40 with dynamic vol scaling then fast/slow vol switching: Sharpe and max drawdown
base_rates.number: Sharpe 0.7 -> 1.0 (1-year half-life vol scaling) -> 1.1 (adds 12-day half-life fast measure that acts only when it diverges from slow); max DD -40% -> -21%; 78% -> 91% of periods inside the 7-13% vol band; turnover x4.4, cost ~7 bps/yr
base_rates.source: Man Group, 'Volatility is Back: Better to Target Returns or Target Risk?' (Harvey/Rattray/Van Hemert line of work)
base_rates.applicability: Practitioner version of (3) for a beta-dominated portfolio; the 12-day fast trigger is the analog of a dial that fires on vol regime change. Applies to the beta the book nets to, not to the reversal alpha.

base_rates.claim: A drawdown-control overlay in the Man/Harvey framework halves maximum drawdown without raising Sharpe; vol targeting raises Sharpe modestly
base_rates.number: Vol targeting Sharpe 1.62 -> 1.79 (+10%) with less negative skew; drawdown control rule: no Sharpe increase, max DD roughly halved (secondary-source summary of the Strategic Risk Management book/AHL research)
base_rates.source: Harvey, Rattray & Van Hemert, Strategic Risk Management (Wiley), summarized via search; primary tables not retrieved
base_rates.applicability: For a principal who explicitly does NOT want a max-drawdown constraint, the drawdown-control rule buys the one thing he says he does not need at zero Sharpe benefit. Weak retrieval quality; treat as directional.

base_rates.claim: Mechanical drawdown cut-off rules on uncorrelated strategies cost return over the long run
base_rates.number: Three uncorrelated Sharpe-0.5 strategies with an automatic exit at a 20% drawdown: the consistent (no-rule) portfolio beat the dynamic portfolio by 2.2%/yr on average over 30 years. Base rates for a Sharpe 0.5, 10% vol strategy: P(20%+ drawdown) ~40% over 5y, ~60% over 10y, ~80% over 25y; a Sharpe 0.6/15% vol strategy can show a 30%+ drawdown lasting 9 years inside 30 years
base_rates.source: Man Group, 'Trend Following and Drawdowns: Is This Time Different?'
base_rates.applicability: Direct evidence against drawdown-triggered de-risking of strategies you believe are good. Consistent with the repo's own ML meta-labeling negative result (win-rate selectivity does not raise expectancy).

base_rates.claim: Stop-loss rules have a NEGATIVE 'stopping premium' under a random walk and a negative first-order effect for MEAN-REVERTING strategies; positive only in proportion to positive autocorrelation (momentum)
base_rates.number: Random walk: stopping premium always < 0. AR(1) with phi<0 (mean reversion): stop-loss hurts expected return to first order. Empirical S&P/bond futures 1993-2011: stops evaluated at monthly intervals +1.5% return, -5% vol, Sharpe up to +20%; daily-frequency stops add nothing. A strategy's hurdle scales with its per-period Sharpe (annual Sharpe 1.0 = monthly 0.29)
base_rates.source: Kaminski & Lo, Journal of Financial Markets 18:234-254
base_rates.applicability: Theory says cutting size after losses is expected-return negative for the dip-buy / OLV / reversal sleeves and can be positive for the breakout sleeves. Matches the repo's stop-arming and no-stop findings (OLV, 3x Leader Gap Fade, Monthly Weak Close) and the 81-episode day-1 stop study (-33R).

base_rates.claim: Raising monthly serial correlation from 0 to +0.1 deepens drawdowns as much as cutting Sharpe from 0.5 to 0.4; drawdown rules are useful for detecting DECAYED managers (Type I/II trade-off), not for sizing a strategy known to be good
base_rates.number: 100,000 simulations of monthly returns; autocorrelation +0.1 ~ Sharpe -0.1 in drawdown terms
base_rates.source: Van Hemert, Ganz, Harvey, Rattray, Sanchez Martin & Yawitch, 'Drawdowns', JPM 46(8):34-50
base_rates.applicability: Base rate for the orchestrator: the book's daily PnL autocorrelation (positions overlap across 1-63 day holds) mechanically fattens drawdowns relative to an iid Sharpe-2 assumption; budget for it rather than throttle on it.

base_rates.claim: Per-stock 10% intra-month stop-loss on momentum tames crashes and more than doubles Sharpe
base_rates.source: Han, Zhou & Zhu, 'Taming Momentum Crashes: A Simple Stop-Loss Strategy'
base_rates.applicability: Per-POSITION stops on momentum-type longs (52wh Breakout, Sector BO, 3x fades on the short side) have support; the same instrument is negative on the reversal sleeves (Kaminski-Lo).

base_rates.claim: Momentum (WML) is a written call on the market in bear states; hedging with EX-ANTE betas does not fix crashes because loser betas jump with the rebound itself
base_rates.number: 1927-2013: WML Sharpe 0.71 vs market 0.40, beta -0.58, alpha 22.3%/yr (t 8.5). Bear-market WML beta 1.13 lower (t -13.4); in bear markets up-market beta -1.51 vs down-market beta -0.70 (t diff 4.5), i.e. -1.80 total on up days; LOSER decile up-beta 2.16 vs down-beta 1.56. Crashes: Jul-Aug 1932 losers +232% vs winners +32%; Mar-May 2009 losers +163% vs winners +8%. Ex-ante 42-day rolling beta hedge 'performs no better than unhedged'; Grundy-Martin ex-post hedge is not implementable. Dynamic strategy (bear indicator + 126-day market variance forecasts) roughly doubles Sharpe; across all markets/assets Sharpe 1.18; Japan 0.07 -> 0.42
base_rates.source: Daniel & Moskowitz, JFE 122(2):221-247 / NBER w20439
base_rates.applicability: Central to (1): a beta hedge sized from trailing beta is exactly the ex-ante hedge that failed, because conditional beta is state- and direction-dependent. This book's dip-buys are LONG past losers, whose up-beta in bear states (2.16) is the payoff; a short-index hedge set on trailing (down) beta 1.56 under-hedges the loss side and gives away the rebound. Crash predictors that DO work are a bear-state indicator plus trailing variance, not vol alone.

base_rates.claim: Scaling momentum by its own trailing 6-month realized vol to a 12% target nearly doubles Sharpe and removes most crash risk
base_rates.source: Barroso & Santa-Clara, JFE 116(1):111-120
base_rates.applicability: Strongest evidence for a sleeve-level vol scaler on the trend/breakout sleeves. Daniel-Moskowitz show a mean+variance dynamic rule beats constant-vol, so a dial that carries a bear-state term should beat pure vol scaling there.

base_rates.claim: Short-term reversal (liquidity provision) returns AND conditional Sharpe rise strongly with VIX; industry-level reversal is unprofitable unconditionally but profitable when VIX is high
base_rates.number: Jan 1998-Dec 2010, individual-stock reversal: 0.30%/day (transaction prices) / 0.18%/day (quote midpoints), annualized Sharpe 8.44 / 4.50 pre-cost; industry reversal 0.02%/day, Sharpe 0.56. Unconditional beta 0.11. Daily return +0.22 pp per 1 pt of normalized VIX (~16 pts annualized VIX), adj R2 0.07; conditional annualized Sharpe +0.13 per 1 pt of annualized VIX (0.08 for industry reversal). Positive skew (3.0), no losing 3-month window 1998-2010 pre-cost; worst 3-month (quote-midpoint) -2.13% vs CRSP VW -52%. Hedging conditional (sign-of-lagged-market) beta: Sharpe 8.44 -> 9.58, std 0.56 -> 0.48%/day, mean unchanged
base_rates.source: Nagel, 'Evaporating Liquidity', RFS 25(7):2005-2039 / NBER w17653
base_rates.applicability: Core support for (2): the risk premium to liquidity provision scales UP with VIX, so a rule that cuts reversal size when the dial is high sells the premium at its peak. Caveats: long-short, daily, pre-cost, 1998-2010, and the hedge that helped was a mechanical sign-of-yesterday beta hedge (the strategy is short high-beta after up days), not a vol-triggered index short.

base_rates.claim: A 5-day reversal strategy's Sharpe varies over time but is UNRELATED to VIX; reversion has a ~2.5-day half-life and has decayed dramatically over time
base_rates.number: 1972-2013 baseline strategy Sharpe 3.08 (pre-cost, their weighting); price overshoot decays with half-life ~2.5 days; time variation in Sharpe 'unrelated to standard measures of market turmoil such as the VIX'
base_rates.source: Collin-Dufresne & Daniel, 'Liquidity and Return Reversals' (working paper)
base_rates.applicability: Direct counter-evidence to Nagel on (2). The 2.5-day half-life also says most of the reversal premium is captured inside a 5-day hold, which matches the ledger's fill-day findings (OLV 89% of fills by T+3, day 4-10 fills add ~0 R).

base_rates.claim: 'Buy the dip' returns on 60/40 and short-VIX are mostly embedded long beta (drift), not timing alpha
base_rates.number: Moderate dips: raw Sharpe 0.72 -> 0.38 after removing drift; severe crashes negative after drift removal; short-VIX severe spikes 125% drift ratio (returns fully explained by accidental SPX beta); 2020 spikes preceded the worst crash in a decade
base_rates.source: CFM, 'The Hidden Beta in Dip Trade'
base_rates.applicability: Says the thing a dial-armed index short would hedge away from FAMILY4/OLV is a large fraction of their return. Consistent with the repo's SPY-hedge study (OLV ~8% SPY-explained overall, 32% at dial>=65; every dial-gated SPY-short variant lost on drift).

base_rates.claim: International equity correlations rise in BEAR markets, not with volatility per se; exceedance correlation grows with the size of the negative threshold and shrinks on the positive side
base_rates.number: Monthly 1959-1996. US-UK: 0.53 at 0%; negative tail 0.58 (-3%), 0.55 (-5%), 0.60 (-8%), 0.68 (-10%); positive tail 0.42 (0%), 0.35 (+3%), 0.36 (+5%), 0.29 (+8%). US-France: 0.85 at -10% vs 0.35 at +0%. Multivariate normality rejected in the negative tail only
base_rates.source: Longin & Solnik, Journal of Finance 56(2):649-676
base_rates.applicability: For (1): correlation (hedge effectiveness) is a function of TREND, not vol. A hedge armed by a vol/positioning dial fires in high-vol bull tapes (2020 recovery, 2021) where correlations are not elevated and drift is positive; a trend/bear-state trigger is the one the correlation evidence supports.

base_rates.claim: US stock-to-market correlations are much higher on the downside than the upside, more so for small, value and past-LOSER stocks; high-beta stocks show less asymmetry
base_rates.number: Downside conditional correlations exceed normal-implied levels by 11.6% (H statistic); asymmetry strongest for small, high B/M and low-past-return stocks
base_rates.source: Ang & Chen, JFE 63:443-494
base_rates.applicability: The book's dip-buys are by construction the past-loser cell with the largest downside-correlation asymmetry, so left-tail clustering across FAMILY4/OLV positions is above what unconditional betas imply. Argues for budgeting the cluster (position count / same-day de-rate) over hedging it.

base_rates.claim: Base rates for maximum drawdown of an iid strategy over long horizons, in units of annualized volatility (multiply by realized book vol)
base_rates.number: Own simulation, 4000 paths, iid normal daily. 23 years: Sharpe 1.0 mean MDD 2.15 vol-units (p90 2.92, p99 3.93); Sharpe 1.5 1.68 (p90 2.20, p99 2.99); Sharpe 2.0 1.38 (p90 1.79, p99 2.36); Sharpe 3.0 1.04. 5 years: Sharpe 2.0 1.01 (p90 1.38). 1 year: Sharpe 2.0 0.65 (p90 0.99). Student-t(4) shocks barely change it (Sharpe 2.0, 23y: 1.42 mean, p99 2.50). P(MDD > 2x annual vol over 23y): 54% at Sharpe 1, 18% at 1.5, 5% at 2
base_rates.source: researcher simulation (scratchpad dd_base_rates.py), Magdon-Ismail & Atiya 2004 framework
base_rates.applicability: If the book runs ~12% realized vol at Sharpe ~2 (6% of full Kelly at Sharpe 2 is ~12% vol), expected worst-of-23y drawdown is ~17%, p90 ~21%, p99 ~28%; the replay's -12.6% at GRM 1.5 sits at the lucky end or realized vol is lower. Every doubling of GRM doubles these dollar numbers linearly; the repo's own replay (maxDD -8.9/-10.8/-12.6/-14.4% at GRM 1.0/1.25/1.5/1.75) scales sub-linearly only because fixed caps clip the tail. Overlapping holds add positive autocorrelation, which the Drawdowns paper says is worth about -0.1 Sharpe of extra drawdown per +0.1.

base_rates.claim: Responsive vol targeting and fast trend reduced exposure ahead of the March 2020 vol peak; strategic rebalancing rules kept an equity underweight at end-Feb 2020
base_rates.number: Qualitative out-of-sample confirmation only (no return figures retrieved): 'responsive volatility targeting reduced positions dramatically ahead of the most volatile period in March 2020'; faster trend and long-short profitability strategies performed well
base_rates.source: Harvey, Hoyle, Rattray & Van Hemert, 'Strategic Risk Management: Out-of-Sample Evidence from the COVID-19 Equity Selloff', SSRN 3655196
base_rates.applicability: Shows a 12-day-type vol trigger does fire in time in a vol-led crash. The same trigger would have cut the book's dip-buy sizing into the 2020 rebound, where Nagel/Daniel-Moskowitz say the reversal payoff sat.

base_rates.claim: Vol-managed factor strategies' benefits have been disappearing in recent samples
base_rates.number: Title-level finding: 'The disappearing profitability of volatility-managed equity factors' (Journal of Financial Markets, 2023); international replication (J. Empirical Finance 2025) also reports weaker and inconsistent gains
base_rates.source: secondary; not fully retrieved
base_rates.applicability: Recency discount on anything adopted from Moreira-Muir.

implications_for_this_book: (1) Dial-armed beta hedge: the outside evidence UNDERCUTS it for the mean-reversion sleeves and only weakly supports it for the breakout sleeves. Daniel-Moskowitz: an ex-ante (trailing-beta) hedge of a strategy whose beta is direction-dependent does not improve returns; the book's dip-buys are long past losers whose bear-state up-beta (2.16) exceeds down-beta (1.56), so any hedge ratio either under-hedges the loss side or sells the rebound that is the trade. CFM: dip-buy returns are largely drift/beta (Sharpe 0.72 -> 0.38 ex-drift), so hedging the beta hedges away the P&L. Longin-Solnik: correlation rises with bear TREND, not with vol, so a hedge armed by a vol/positioning dial (dial 89.5 in Aug-2026 with SPY above its 200-SMA and OLV only trading above the 200-SMA) fires in the wrong state; the repo's own finding that every dial-gated SPY-short variant lost on drift is what this literature predicts. If a hedge exists at all, arm it on a bear-state/trend condition (Daniel-Moskowitz's crash predictor is bear indicator x 126-day variance), size it to the RESIDUAL beta after the reversal sleeves' mechanical short-high-beta tilt (Nagel's hedge that helped was sign-of-yesterday beta, and it added Sharpe only by cutting variance, mean unchanged), and apply it to the breakout/momentum sleeves where crash risk is option-like and documented.

(2) Sizing mean-reversion UP in high VIX: supported by Nagel (conditional Sharpe +0.13 per VIX point; industry reversal profitable only in high VIX; no losing 3-month window incl. 2008) and by Daniel-Moskowitz's loser-decile up-betas, contested by Collin-Dufresne-Daniel (no VIX relation for a 5-day reversal 1972-2013) and by Moreira-Muir (the long-beta leg's E[R]/Var falls in high vol). Synthesis for this book: the liquidity-provision component of FAMILY4/OLV/St-OS-Sznl deserves flat-to-UP risk-unit sizing when VIX is high, while the beta component argues for keeping NOTIONAL from growing. ATR-unit sizing already does most of this (constant risk units = shrinking notional as vol rises). The literature therefore argues against the FAMILY4 0.25x cut at dial>=50 as a default and for the P/C-fear 'full size in washout' branch; the repo's PIT evidence (FAMILY4 hi -0.10 vs lo +0.63, t=-1.96, 9 years, 6/9 negative) is the in-sample counterweight and is not strong enough to override a documented external base rate on its own. A defensible middle: keep risk-unit size at 1.0x in high VIX when the tape is a bear-state washout (trend down + fear ON), keep the cut only when high vol coincides with bull trend and low fear (the state Longin-Solnik and Nagel do not cover and the ledger says is bad).

(3) Book-level vol target: the evidence does NOT support a single scalar on this book. Vol management works OOS for momentum (UMD 0.47 -> 1.04, Barroso 0.53 -> 0.97, Bongaerts momentum DD 54% -> 20%) and fails or hurts OOS for the market/beta leg (MKT 0.53 -> 0.41) and for most other anomalies (Cederburg 103, Barroso-Detzel net of costs); it would explicitly cut liquidity-provision sleeves at the moment their premium peaks (Nagel). Position-level ATR sizing plus per-strategy 250 bps/day cap is already an inverse-vol scheme, so a book target double-counts. If a regime scaler is wanted, the supported form is (a) sleeve-level, on 52wh Breakout / Sector BO / trend-like longs, (b) two-state extreme-quintile (Bongaerts) rather than continuous, (c) with a bear-state term (Daniel-Moskowitz), and (d) never on the dip-buy/OLV sleeves. This is consistent with the repo's dead book-wide throttle (PIT t=-0.23).

Drawdown-triggered de-risking: rejected by theory for mean-reverting strategies (Kaminski-Lo: negative stopping premium under random walk and to first order under mean reversion), by practitioner simulation (Man: -2.2%/yr vs no-rule over 30y), and by ETF studies (Varma: 10/15/20% cutoffs rarely help). Supported only as per-position stops on momentum-type longs (Han-Zhou-Zhu) and as a manager-decay detector (Van Hemert et al.), which for this book means a strategy-retirement trigger on multi-year underperformance, not a size throttle after a bad month.

Drawdown budget instead of drawdown constraint: at Sharpe ~2 and ~12% realized vol, the 23-year expected max DD is ~1.4x annual vol (~17%), p90 ~1.8x (~21%), p99 ~2.4x (~28%), fat tails barely change it; overlapping holds add positive PnL autocorrelation worth roughly a 0.1-Sharpe-equivalent of extra drawdown per +0.1 autocorrelation. The principal's acceptance of a larger drawdown should be stated as a vol level (or GRM), and the GRM replay's sub-linear maxDD scaling should be read as cap clipping, not as free lunch: at GRM 3.0 the iid base rate is a ~35% expected worst drawdown with a 1-in-10 chance of ~42%.

Seasonality/timing of sizing by signal flow: the momentum-crash literature says the dangerous state for trend/breakout sleeves is 'market down over 1-2 years AND trailing variance high' (both terms independently forecast WML), and the vol-management literature says calm-tape periods are where risk-asset beta is cheapest per unit variance; so up-sizing the breakout sleeves in calm bull tapes and down-sizing them in bear-state high-variance tapes has two independent literatures behind it, while the reverse (up-size dip-buys in bear-state washouts) has Nagel plus the repo's P/C-fear logic and one contradicting paper.

Conditional-correlation budgeting: Ang-Chen's asymmetry is largest exactly in the past-loser cell the dip-buys live in, and Longin-Solnik's tail correlations reach 0.7-0.85 in the -10% monthly tail vs ~0.3-0.4 in the +tail; treat concurrent FAMILY4/OLV/3x-Bear-Fade positions as one bet in bear trends (same-day de-rate, position-count caps) rather than relying on cross-ticker diversification or an index hedge.
contested_points: Whether volatility management adds real-time value at all: Moreira-Muir (2017) alpha 4.86%/yr and +25% Sharpe vs Cederburg et al. (2020) 'generally lower OOS Sharpe and CER' and Barroso-Detzel (2021) 'zero net alpha except the market'; DeMiguel et al. (2024) partially rehabilitate it only as a conditional MULTIfactor allocation (+13% OOS net Sharpe) while confirming single-factor failure for MKT/SMB/CMA.

Reversal returns vs VIX: Nagel (2012, 1998-2010 daily, pre-cost) finds Sharpe rises 0.13 per VIX point; Collin-Dufresne & Daniel (2016, 1972-2013, 5-day) find the time variation unrelated to VIX. Difference plausibly from horizon (daily vs 5-day), sample (crisis-heavy 1998-2010) and construction; the book's 5-10 day holds sit closer to Collin-Dufresne-Daniel.

What triggers correlation increases: Longin-Solnik say bear trend, not volatility per se; most practitioner risk dials (including this repo's fragility dial) are vol/positioning based. Ang-Chen frame it as downside moves generally.

Drawdown control: Man's book-level summary claims the rule halves max DD at unchanged Sharpe, Man's 2025 note finds a 20% cut-off rule costs 2.2%/yr, Kaminski-Lo make it sign-dependent on autocorrelation. Primary tables for the book/AHL rule were not retrievable (SSRN/Man pages blocked); those numbers are secondary-source.

Cederburg in-sample count: secondary summaries report managed Sharpe higher in 53/103 vs 63/103 strategies; the primary PDF could not be text-extracted. Both agree only ~8 are consistently better and OOS is negative on average.

Momentum beta hedging: Grundy-Martin (2001) ex-post hedge doubles pre-WWII Sharpe; Daniel-Moskowitz show the ex-ante version does nothing. Relevant to whether ANY implementable hedge of a state-dependent-beta strategy can work.
Conditional vol targeting (Bongaerts 2020) is designed and evaluated in-sample; no expanding-window test, so Cederburg's structural-instability critique applies to it too.
Quantpedia's illustrative Sharpe table (0.79 -> 1.02 simple, 0.90 -> 1.34 EWMA, DD -31% -> -19%) has unclear provenance and is not from the Harvey et al. paper tables; excluded from base rates.

Recency: 'disappearing profitability of volatility-managed equity factors' (2023) and international replications (2025) suggest the in-sample gains have decayed post-publication, which also applies to the momentum sleeve result that is otherwise the most robust.

outside_evidence.topic: Broker margin and capacity boundaries for a short-horizon US equity long/short book at IBKR portfolio margin (gross-notional ceiling, liquidation mechanics, market-impact base rates, ADV participation thresholds)

base_rates.claim: IBKR Portfolio Margin (TIMS) standardized stress for stock, equity options, narrow-based indices and single stock futures
base_rates.number: +/-15%, with eight other points inside the range; margin = worst-case loss across the stress grid
base_rates.source: Interactive Brokers, Stock Margin Requirements / Portfolio Margin Mechanics (interactivebrokers.co.uk, page fetched 2026-09)
base_rates.applicability: Directly sets the maintenance requirement on every single-stock leg in this book: ~15% of position notional for an unhedged long or short. Implies a hard gross ceiling of 1/0.15 = 6.67x NAV.

base_rates.claim: TIMS stress for broad-based / growth indices (SPY, QQQ, index proxies)
base_rates.number: +6% / -8% plus eight intermediate points; broad-based index implied vol shocked +/-75% (other classes +/-150%)
base_rates.source: Interactive Brokers, Portfolio Margin Mechanics
base_rates.applicability: Index-ETF legs (SPY/QQQ dip-buys, the 25% NAV exposure leg, event sleeve SPY/IWM) are margined at ~8% of notional, roughly half the single-stock rate: 12.5x gross capacity per index dollar vs 6.67x per stock dollar.

base_rates.claim: TIMS stress for US small-cap and FINRA market indices
base_rates.number: +10% / -10% plus eight intermediate points
base_rates.source: Interactive Brokers, Portfolio Margin Mechanics
base_rates.applicability: IWM-type legs sit between index and single stock (~10% requirement).

base_rates.claim: Leveraged ETFs under portfolio margin: the standard market moves are multiplied by the ETF's stated leverage factor
base_rates.source: OCC Customer Portfolio Margin scenario table as summarized on Wikipedia 'Portfolio margin' (fetched 2026-09)
base_rates.applicability: SQQQ/TQQQ/DUST/JDST legs in the two 3x Overbot Fades and the 3x Leader Gap Fade consume ~3x the margin per dollar of notional. Because their ATR is also ~3x, margin per unit of ATR risk is roughly INVARIANT to leverage under PM (see rules-based caveat below).

base_rates.claim: IBKR rules-based (Reg-T) maintenance for leveraged ETFs
base_rates.number: Long: min(25% x leverage factor, 100%) = 75% for 3x. Short: min(30% x leverage factor, 100%) = 90% for 3x
base_rates.source: Interactive Brokers, Stock Margin Requirements disclosures (interactivebrokers.co.uk, fetched 2026-09)
base_rates.applicability: A short 3x bear-ETF leg costs 90% of notional under rules-based margin vs 45% under TIMS. IBKR's own page states it 'will calculate both methodologies and assess the higher of the two' for some client categories, and separately that 'IBKR house margin requirements may be greater than rule-based margin'. Worst case a $100k SQQQ short ties up $90k, i.e. margin per unit of ATR risk DOUBLES vs a single stock.

base_rates.claim: Portfolio margin concentration minimum
base_rates.number: Classes with large single concentrations get a 30% margin requirement applied to the concentrated position (vs the 15% single-stock stress)
base_rates.source: Interactive Brokers, Portfolio Margin Mechanics
base_rates.applicability: A concentrated leg's capacity halves (6.67x -> 3.33x). IBKR does not publish the concentration trigger; third-party summaries put it near a single name exceeding ~50% of the portfolio. The OLV book at ~84% of NAV in 10 names on 2026-08-24 is exactly the shape that attracts this.

base_rates.claim: Portfolio margin other minimums
base_rates.number: Initial margin = 110% of maintenance margin; $0.375 x index per-contract minimum; Reg-T special requirements for OTCBB, Pink Sheet and low-cap stocks still apply under PM
base_rates.source: Interactive Brokers, Portfolio Margin Mechanics
base_rates.applicability: New positions need 10% more margin than held ones - a book at exactly the maintenance ceiling cannot add. Directly bounds the ~870-name overflow tier where low-cap special requirements bite.

base_rates.claim: Shares-outstanding concentration algorithm
base_rates.number: Nominal margin increased for positions >1% of a company's shares outstanding; FULL (100%) margin required at >=9% of shares outstanding for stocks, >=5% for ETFs
base_rates.source: Interactive Brokers, Stock Margin Requirements disclosures
base_rates.applicability: Irrelevant at $750k notional except in micro-cap overflow names and thin 3x ETFs; the ETF 5% threshold is the one worth checking on small leveraged products.

base_rates.claim: Reg-T short-stock minimums (which also carry into PM for low-priced names)
base_rates.number: 30% of market value if price > $16.67; $5.00/share if $5.00 < price <= $16.67; 100% of market value if price < $5.00; $2.50/share if price <= $2.50
base_rates.source: Interactive Brokers, Stock Margin Requirements (US stocks table)
base_rates.applicability: Overbot-Vol-Spike and 3x fade shorts in sub-$17 names are margined per-share, not per-percent: a $6 stock short costs $5/share = 83% of notional. Cheap-stock shorts are 5x more margin-expensive than the 15% headline.

base_rates.claim: Portfolio margin minimum equity
base_rates.number: USD 110,000 NLV to open; below USD 100,000 the account is restricted from margin-increasing trades; below the $100k minimum a margin surcharge phases the account back toward Reg-T levels
base_rates.source: Interactive Brokers, Portfolio Margin Eligibility
base_rates.applicability: Primary account (~$632k NLV) has ~5.3x headroom to the restriction line; the PA (~$66k) is BELOW the PM minimum and is presumably Reg-T. A 84% NAV drawdown would be needed to hit the restriction on the primary.

base_rates.claim: Achievable leverage under portfolio margin vs Reg T
base_rates.number: 'leverage of 6.67 or more' on equities vs ~2:1 under Reg T
base_rates.source: Interactive Brokers / Wikipedia 'Portfolio margin'
base_rates.applicability: 6.67x = 1/0.15 is the arithmetic ceiling for a single-stock book with no offsets. Stocks get NO cross-class offsets in TIMS ('for stocks and Single Stock Futures offsets are only allowed within a class'), so a long/short book is margined on GROSS, not net - hedging does not buy capacity.

base_rates.claim: IBKR house gross-leverage limitation
base_rates.number: Gross Position Value not more than 30 times Net Liquidation Value (minus futures options value)
base_rates.source: Interactive Brokers, Margin Requirements page (via search summary, 2026)
base_rates.applicability: Non-binding here: 30x is far above the 6.67x TIMS wall for a stock book. Cited only to close off the 'is there a separate gross cap' question.

base_rates.claim: Soft Edge Margin tolerance and its expiry
base_rates.number: From the start of the trading day until 15 minutes before the close, a margin deficit within 10% of NLV is tolerated; when SEM ends the FULL maintenance requirement must be met
base_rates.source: Interactive Brokers, Margin Calculations for Securities (via search, 2026)
base_rates.applicability: The real liquidation clock is ~15:45 ET. A book that is 5-10% deficient intraday is fine until 15:45 and then auto-liquidated. Strategies whose exits are MOC / next-open (OLV vol-confirm, event sleeve MOC) are exposed at exactly this moment.

base_rates.claim: IBKR liquidation mechanics
base_rates.number: IBKR does not issue margin calls; liquidations are automated and in real time, with no warning before positions are closed
base_rates.source: Interactive Brokers, Margin Requirements / IBKR Campus glossary (2026)
base_rates.applicability: There is no cure period. Any sizing plan must hold the maintenance requirement with a buffer under a same-day adverse move, because the recovery mechanism is the broker selling your worst positions at the worst time.

base_rates.claim: Reg-T end-of-day enforcement time
base_rates.number: Reg T initial requirement (50% long) enforced at the end of the trading day, 3:50 PM ET, via the SMA calculation; a negative end-of-day SMA subjects the account to liquidation
base_rates.source: Interactive Brokers, Margin Calculations for Securities (via search, 2026)
base_rates.applicability: Applies to the Reg-T (PA) account, not the PM account. PM requirements are TIMS-based and static intraday (OCC disseminates once per night) but compliance is recomputed intraday on live prices.

base_rates.claim: Exposure fee: stress-based surcharge on risky accounts
base_rates.number: Daily fee for accounts whose average stress-scenario loss exceeds account equity; IBKR began charging accounts adversely affected by a 1-day 30% equity-market drop; the fee is deducted from cash and if that deduction creates a deficiency, the account is liquidated; greater of exposure fee and inventory fee is charged
base_rates.source: Interactive Brokers, 'Exposure Fee for High Risk Accounts' (page fetched 2026-09) + Elite Trader/forum reporting of the 30% scenario
base_rates.applicability: A soft ceiling well BELOW the 6.67x margin wall. A book with net long exposure above ~1.0x NAV, or with concentrated single names, fails a -30% scenario on equity and starts paying a daily fee. IBKR names concentrated single positions as the main driver and diversification/hedging as the cure.

base_rates.claim: Precedent for firm-wide house margin increases in stress
base_rates.number: Ahead of the Nov 2020 US election IBKR raised margin requirements by as much as 35% above normal, phased in daily from Sept 28 to Oct 23, 2020
base_rates.source: CNBC, 'Interactive Brokers braces for election volatility...' (2020-09-23)
base_rates.applicability: A 35% house uplift turns the 15% stock requirement into 20.25% and the gross ceiling from 6.67x to 4.94x. Any plan running above ~4x gross can be forced to delever by the broker's calendar, not the market's.

base_rates.claim: Precedent for name-level house action
base_rates.number: Jan 2021: AMC, BB, EXPR, GME, KOSS put into liquidation-only for options with long stock at 100% margin and SHORT stock at 300% margin
base_rates.source: Interactive Brokers press release via Business Wire (2021-01-28)
base_rates.applicability: Direct hazard for the short book (OVS, 3x fades, overflow shorts). A 300% requirement on a $100k short demands $300k of margin overnight with no notice. Position-level tail risk that no ATR stop covers.

base_rates.claim: Square-root law of market impact
base_rates.number: I = Y * sigma_daily * sqrt(Q/ADV), with Y an O(1) constant calibrated in the 0.5-1.0 range and the exponent delta empirically 0.4-0.7 (0.5 for small ticks, 0.6 for large ticks)
base_rates.source: Toth et al. (2011), Bershova & Rakhlin (2013), Bouchaud 'The Square-Root Law of Market Impact' (substack, 2023)
base_rates.applicability: The workhorse. For this book: impact per side in bps = Y * sigma% * sqrt(participation). Impact is approximately independent of execution schedule and of N child orders, so slicing does not escape it - only trading less does.

base_rates.claim: Square-root law benchmark magnitudes at 1% of daily volume
base_rates.number: Bouchaud benchmark stock: 1% of daily volume -> 5 bps. Kyle-Obizhaeva calibration: 1% ADV -> 20 bps for a stock with 200 bps daily volatility
base_rates.source: Bouchaud (2023); Kyle & Obizhaeva, Market Microstructure Invariance (Econometrica 2016) / 'The Market Impact Puzzle'
base_rates.applicability: Anchors Y*sigma: 5-20 bps at 1% ADV spans essentially the whole plausible range. Use 10-20 bps at 1% ADV for a 2-3% ATR name as the working number.

base_rates.claim: Almgren, Thum, Hauptmann & Li fitted impact model
base_rates.number: Permanent impact linear in block size with gamma = 0.314 +/- 0.041 (t=7.7); temporary impact a 3/5 power law with eta = 0.142 +/- 0.0062 (t=23). Square-root temporary impact REJECTED in favor of 3/5. Fit on ~700k Citigroup US orders, Dec 2001-Jun 2003, 29,509 after filters; median order 0.62% of ADV, median duration ~half an hour
base_rates.source: Almgren, Thum, Hauptmann, Li, 'Direct Estimation of Equity Market Impact', Risk (2005)
base_rates.applicability: Their own filter note matters: 'Orders larger than a few percent of daily volume have substantial sources of uncertainty that are not modeled here.' The model is calibrated exactly in the 0.25-1.5% ADV band this book operates in.

base_rates.claim: Almgren et al. worked example: buying 10% of a day's average volume in two large caps
base_rates.number: IBM (ADV 6.561M sh, daily vol 1.57%): permanent 20 bps, temporary 22/15/8 bps at 0.1/0.2/0.5-day duration, realized cost 32/25/18 bps. DRI (ADV 1.929M sh, daily vol 2.26%): permanent 22 bps, temporary 32/21/12 bps, realized cost 43/32/23 bps
base_rates.source: Almgren et al. (2005), Table 3
base_rates.applicability: 10% of ADV in a large cap costs 18-43 bps all-in depending on urgency. This is the empirical anchor for 'how bad does it get' and it is far cheaper than folklore. Note the sample is pre-decimalization-era liquidity; modern electronic markets are cheaper still per FIM below.

base_rates.claim: Frazzini, Israel & Moskowitz live institutional execution costs
base_rates.number: $1.7tn of live trades, 19 developed markets, 1998-2016 (earlier draft 1998-2011). Mean market impact 12.18 bps, mean implementation shortfall 13 bps, opportunity cost 0.82 bps. Value-weighted 18.65 bps market impact / 20.20 bps shortfall. Mean trade $695,300, median $401,500. ~70% of initial impact is permanent (only ~2.5 of 9 bps reverses within 24h)
base_rates.source: Frazzini, Israel & Moskowitz, 'Trading Costs of Asset Pricing Anomalies' / 'Trading Costs' (SSRN 2294498, 3229719)
base_rates.applicability: Median institutional trade ($400k) is the same order as this book's per-position notional ($50-150k). Costs of ~12-20 bps per side are the realistic base rate for actively executed orders, an order of magnitude below the academic effective-spread proxies.

base_rates.claim: FIM cost split by market cap and by trade direction
base_rates.number: Large cap 11.21 bps of market impact vs small cap 21.27 bps. Long-only trades ~16 bps vs long-short ~10 bps. In the US, selling short is 2.67 bps CHEAPER than selling long (not statistically significant); buying to cover is more expensive than buying long
base_rates.source: Frazzini, Israel & Moskowitz (2012/2018)
base_rates.applicability: Overflow (small/mid) tier costs roughly 2x the liquid tier per trade. The short book is not systematically more expensive to enter - the asymmetry is on the cover.

base_rates.claim: FIM fitted trading-cost regression (cost in bps)
base_rates.number: Coefficient on sqrt(fraction of daily volume, in %) = 5.61 to 8.77 (t 2.24-5.69); linear fraction-of-volume 0.71-1.68; log(ME in $bn) -2.05 to -5.55; idiosyncratic vol +0.10 to +0.19; VIX +0.25 to +0.43. R-squared ~7%
base_rates.source: Frazzini, Israel & Moskowitz, Table V
base_rates.applicability: Read directly: ~7.4 bps per sqrt(% of ADV), so 0.1% ADV -> ~2.3 bps, 1% -> ~8 bps, 4% -> ~15 bps, plus a size term. Also: cost rises with VIX at ~0.36 bps per VIX point, so a scan firing at VIX 40 costs ~9 bps more per trade than at VIX 15.

base_rates.claim: FIM capacity: short-term reversal is the worst-capacity anomaly they study
base_rates.number: STR turnover 305% per month, market impact 18.4 bps per trade, realized cost 6.75%/yr, implied fund size at their manager's scale $1.51bn. Break-even fund size (US, all stocks 1926-2011) $9.45bn vs $354bn for SMB, $190bn for HML, $66bn for UMD. International $3.30bn; global $12.75bn. Trading constraint imposed in the optimization: fraction of daily volume <= 5%
base_rates.source: Frazzini, Israel & Moskowitz, Tables VII/IX
base_rates.applicability: The academic 1-month reversal - the closest published cousin of the dip-buy family - breaks even at ~$9bn US. That is ~12,000x this book's NAV. Capacity is NOT the binding constraint at $750k; it becomes one somewhere in the tens of millions for the liquid tier and far sooner in overflow.

base_rates.claim: Novy-Marx & Velikov after-cost returns for reversal strategies
base_rates.number: Short-run reversals: gross 0.37%/mo, turnover 90.87%/mo, T-costs 1.65%, NET -1.28%/mo (t -6.02). Industry-relative reversals: gross 0.98%, cost 1.78%, net -0.80% (t -4.73). With 10%/50% banding mitigation STR: gross 0.28%, cost 1.00%, net -0.72%. By size (net): large -0.51%, small -0.84%, micro -1.90%/mo. Mid-turnover anomaly execution costs 20-57 bps
base_rates.source: Novy-Marx & Velikov, 'A Taxonomy of Anomalies and Their Trading Costs', RFS 29(1) (2016)
base_rates.applicability: Flatly negative net returns for naive reversal at institutional scale, with TAQ effective-spread costing. The sharp contradiction with FIM (which finds STR viable at ~$1.5bn) is a cost-measurement dispute, not a data dispute - see contested points. Both agree the family has the LOWEST capacity of any documented anomaly.

base_rates.claim: Nagel: unconditional reversal-strategy statistics on the 500 largest caps
base_rates.number: Transaction-price version: mean +0.30%/day, sd 0.56%/day, annualized Sharpe 8.44, beta 0.11, worst day -3.88%, worst 3-month +2.56%. Quote-midpoint version: mean +0.18%/day, Sharpe 4.50. Industry-portfolio reversal: +0.02%/day, Sharpe 0.56. CRSP VW index over the same sample: +0.02%/day, sd 1.35%
base_rates.source: Nagel, 'Evaporating Liquidity', RFS 25(7) (2012), Table 1
base_rates.applicability: The 0.30 vs 0.18 gap IS the bid-ask capture: ~12 bps/day of the gross return is liquidity provision, not prediction. This book's persistent limit entries (close - 0.25 ATR) harvest part of that; its MOO/MOC exits pay it away. Nagel is explicit that fixed costs of high-speed access, not risk, are what keep the Sharpe from being arbitraged.

base_rates.claim: Nagel: reversal expected returns and conditional Sharpe rise with VIX
base_rates.number: Expected returns and conditional Sharpe ratios 'increase enormously' with VIX; VIX is a much stronger predictor than lagged market returns; the relation survives standardizing returns by conditional volatility
base_rates.source: Nagel, 'Evaporating Liquidity', RFS (2012)
base_rates.applicability: Outside evidence says the liquidity-provision leg of a dip-buy book should be sized UP, not down, when volatility spikes - the opposite direction from the repo's FAMILY4 frag_risk_bands [[50,999,0.25]]. Flagged as a contested point rather than a recommendation, because the repo cut is PIT-validated on this specific book.

base_rates.claim: Avramov, Chordia & Goyal on reversal capacity
base_rates.number: Largest reversals and contrarian profits occur in high-turnover, low-liquidity stocks; contrarian profits are SMALLER than likely transaction costs in exactly those names
base_rates.source: Avramov, Chordia & Goyal, 'Liquidity and Autocorrelations in Individual Stock Returns', Journal of Finance 61(5) 2365-2394 (2006)
base_rates.applicability: The tier where the signal is strongest (overflow small caps) is the tier where impact eats it. Independent corroboration of the overflow-tier impact warning below.

base_rates.claim: Post-2005 anomaly net returns generally
base_rates.number: Across 204 anomalies, mean long-short return net of costs is ~-1 bp/month post-2005 under original implementations, rising to ~+4 bps under cost-minimizing execution; gross returns decay ~50% post-publication
base_rates.source: Chen & Velikov, 'Zeroing In on the Expected Returns of Anomalies', JFQA 58(3) 968-1004 (2023)
base_rates.applicability: Base rate for how much of a documented short-horizon edge survives costs at scale. It says: assume the published version of anything in this family is dead net of costs, and that anything alive is alive because of execution design (passive entries, banded rebalancing, ADV limits) rather than signal strength.

base_rates.claim: Dai, Medhat, Novy-Marx & Rizova on the structure of reversals
base_rates.number: Higher volatility -> faster, initially stronger reversals; lower turnover -> more persistent, ultimately stronger reversals; average reversal returns 'have come down over the last 20 years, consistent with improved market liquidity'; a standalone reversal strategy is 'impractical because it will have extremely high turnover and trading costs'
base_rates.source: Dai, Medhat, Novy-Marx & Rizova, 'Reversals and the Returns to Liquidity Provision', Financial Analysts Journal 80(2) 122-151 (2024); Dimensional Q&A (2024)
base_rates.applicability: Supports conditioning hold length on volatility (high-vol names reverse faster - shorter holds) and turnover (low-turnover names reverse more persistently - longer holds), and supports the book's design of reversal as a SCREEN inside selective entries rather than a standalone high-turnover sleeve.

base_rates.claim: Derived: impact cost expressed in R units is volatility-invariant
base_rates.number: cost_roundtrip / R = 2 * Y * (sigma/ATR%) * sqrt(p) / k. With Y=0.75, sigma ~ 0.8*ATR%, k=1.25 ATR stop: cost/R ~= 0.96 * sqrt(participation). So p=0.25% -> 0.05R; p=1% -> 0.10R; p=4% -> 0.19R; p=10% -> 0.30R; p=25% -> 0.48R
base_rates.source: Derived from the square-root law (Toth/Bouchaud calibration) applied to this book's stop-defined risk unit
base_rates.applicability: ATR cancels out. The participation threshold is therefore the SAME for a 2% ATR mega-cap and a 7% ATR 3x ETF. At an edge of 0.3-0.8R, impact reaches 20% of edge at p = 0.4% (weak strategies) to 2.8% (strong ones), and equals the entire edge at p = 10% to 70% of ADV.

base_rates.claim: Derived: margin consumed per dollar of ATR risk
base_rates.number: M/R = TIMS_rate / (k * ATR%). Single stock at 15%, 1.25 ATR stop, 2.5% ATR: $4.80 of margin per $1 of ATR risk. 3x ETF under PM (45% stress, 7.5% ATR): also $4.80. 3x ETF short under rules-based (90%): $9.60. Sub-$17 stock short at $5/share on a $10 stock (50% of notional): $16.00
base_rates.source: Derived from IBKR TIMS/Reg-T rates above
base_rates.applicability: Under PM, leverage factor is margin-neutral per unit of risk; cheap-stock shorts are 3x more margin-expensive per unit of risk than the headline suggests. Concurrent open ATR risk of 300-600 bps of the $750k base ($22k-$45k) consumes only ~$108k-$216k of margin, i.e. 17-34% of a $632k NAV.

implications_for_this_book: GROSS-NOTIONAL CEILING, layered. (a) Arithmetic wall: TIMS gives no long/short offset for stocks, so the requirement is on GROSS. 1/0.15 = 6.67x NAV is the absolute maximum with zero excess liquidity - unreachable in practice. (b) Survivability wall: solvency after a same-day book loss d requires Gross <= (1 - d)/0.15 x NAV. Sizing to survive the repo's own uncapped worst day (-15.75% NAV) gives 5.6x; sizing to survive a 35%-style IBKR house uplift (15% -> 20.25%) plus that loss gives (1-0.1575)/0.2025 = 4.2x. (c) Exposure-fee wall, the real one: IBKR stress-tests a 1-day 30% equity drop against account equity, so NET long exposure much above ~1.0x NAV starts paying a daily fee whose deduction can itself trigger liquidation. RECOMMENDATION: operating ceiling 2.5x gross / 1.0x net of NAV, hard stop at 4.0x gross. That is 3-5x MORE gross than the book currently runs (OLV alone peaked ~$628k = ~1.0x NAV on 2026-08-24, whole-book gross presumably 1.2-1.5x). Margin is not the binding constraint today; it becomes binding around 2.5x gross.

BLENDED-RATE ADJUSTMENT for the 3x sleeves. Blended requirement = 0.15*(stock share) + 0.45*(3x share) + 0.08*(index share) under PM. A book with 20% of gross in 3x ETFs runs a blended 21% and a ceiling of 4.8x rather than 6.67x. If IBKR applies the higher of rules-based and PM to any 3x leg (90% short / 75% long), a 20% 3x share pushes the blended rate to 0.30 and the ceiling to 3.3x. Recommendation: compute headroom off the rules-based 3x rate, not the PM rate, until verified in the live account's margin report.

THE LIQUIDATION CLOCK IS 15:45 ET, NOT 16:00. Soft Edge Margin tolerates a deficit up to 10% of NLV intraday and then expires 15 minutes before the close, at which point the full requirement applies and IBKR auto-liquidates with no call and no warning. Three of this book's exits land inside or after that window: the OVS Friday EOD-DD at 15:58, the (now disabled) OLV book-cap MOC at 15:40-15:58, and every event-sleeve MOC. A sizing plan that raises gross must add a pre-15:30 margin-headroom check, because at 15:45 the broker's liquidation is indiscriminate about which strategy's leg it kills.

NO-RESTING-STOP STRATEGIES ARE MARGIN-UNPROTECTED. OLV has no stop leg (vol-confirmed next-open exit), OVS has use_stop_loss=False, Monthly Weak Close and the 3x Leader Gap Fade have no stop by design. Under auto-liquidation, the broker becomes the de-facto stop and it fires on the aggregate, not the leg. This argues for keeping a hard aggregate-gross cap (the retired 100%-NAV OLV book cap was directionally right even though its trigger was appetite, not evidence) rather than relying on per-leg risk units.

MARGIN PER UNIT OF ATR RISK IS ~$4.80 UNDER PM AND IS INVARIANT TO THE LEVERAGE FACTOR. This is a genuinely useful result for cross-strategy sizing: under portfolio margin a 3x ETF leg consumes the same margin per unit of ATR risk as a single-stock leg, because the TIMS stress scales with the leverage factor exactly as ATR does. So there is NO margin reason to under-size the 3x fades relative to the single-stock strategies. The two exceptions that DO deserve a margin haircut are (i) short 3x under rules-based margin (2x the margin per unit of risk) and (ii) shorts in sub-$17 stocks, where the per-share minimums ($5/share under $16.67, 100% under $5) can cost 3x the margin per unit of risk.

PARTICIPATION THRESHOLD, the number the brief asked for: impact reaches ~20% of per-trade edge at p = (0.2 * edge_in_R / 0.96)^2 of ADV. For the book's stated 0.3-0.8R range that is p = 0.4% of ADV for the weakest strategies, 1.1% at 0.5R, and 2.8% at 0.8R. RECOMMENDED HARD RULE: single-order notional <= 1.0% of 21-day median dollar ADV, with a tighter 0.4% band for any strategy whose ledger avgR is under 0.4R, and an absolute refusal above 5% (FIM's own optimization constraint). Above ~10% of ADV impact consumes the entire edge of a 0.3R strategy.

THE LIQUID TIER HAS 20-40x HEADROOM; THE OVERFLOW TIER IS AT THE BOUNDARY NOW. A typical position (52.5 bps effective risk on $750k, 1.25 ATR stop, 2.5% ATR) is ~$126k of notional. In a $500M-ADV liquid name that is 0.025% of ADV = ~2 bps of impact per side, essentially free, and the position could grow ~40x before hitting the 1% rule. In an overflow name with $10M ADV it is 1.26% of ADV = ~25 bps per side, ~0.16R round trip, i.e. a third of a 0.5R edge already gone. In a $5M-ADV name it is 2.5% of ADV. CONCRETE PROPOSAL: make the ADV participation cap tier-aware - the existing cap should be re-expressed as a hard 1.0% of median-dollar-ADV constraint that BINDS in overflow and never binds in liquid, and any book-wide size increase should be routed to the liquid tier and to index legs, not proportionally across tiers.

THE OVERFLOW TIER IS DOUBLY PENALIZED and the outside evidence agrees with the repo's own survivorship caveat. FIM: small-cap impact 21.3 bps vs 11.2 bps large-cap. Avramov-Chordia-Goyal: reversal profits are largest exactly in high-turnover, low-liquidity names AND smaller than the transaction costs there. Novy-Marx & Velikov: net reversal returns by size are -0.51%/mo large, -0.84% small, -1.90% micro. Combined with the ledger's known delisting survivorship bias, the honest prior on overflow-tier avgR is materially below the backtest, and the correct sizing response is to hold overflow nominal bps flat (or cut) while any book-wide risk increase goes to the liquid tier.

PASSIVE ENTRY IS A REAL AND UNDER-COUNTED EDGE SOURCE. Nagel's decomposition (0.30%/day on transaction prices vs 0.18%/day on quote midpoints) says roughly 12 bps/day of the raw reversal return is bid-ask capture. This book's dominant entry form - a persistent limit at close - 0.25 ATR, filling only when the market comes to it - is on the earning side of that spread, while its MOO/MOC exits and stop-outs pay it. Implication for the sizing plan: strategies with limit entries and time exits (OLV, Monday Dip, MonFri Reversion, Monthly Weak Close) have materially LOWER effective impact than the FIM/NMV base rates imply and can carry larger participation than strategies that both enter and exit at the market (event sleeve, MOO/MOC pitch legs, OVS gap entries). A cost-aware sizing plan should charge market-order strategies ~2x the impact of limit-entry strategies.

VOLATILITY-CONDITIONED SIZING: THE OUTSIDE EVIDENCE POINTS THE OTHER WAY FROM THE REPO'S FAMILY4 BAND. Nagel (2012) finds reversal expected returns AND conditional Sharpe rise strongly with VIX, and reads the whole strategy as compensation for liquidity provision that spikes when intermediaries withdraw. FIM finds trading costs also rise with VIX (+0.36 bps per VIX point), so the correct high-volatility response is arguably 'same or larger size, wider limits, more passive execution', not '0.25x'. The repo's PIT-validated FAMILY4 cut (hi -0.10R vs lo +0.63R, clustered t -1.96) is specific to this book's dial and should not be overturned on outside evidence - but the P/C-fear-ON exception the repo already ships (full or 1.25x size when positioning is washed out) is exactly the Nagel mechanism, and it is the piece with outside support. Recommendation to the orchestrator: treat the fear-conditioned band as the evidence-aligned form and consider whether the OFF-state zeroing at dial>=50 is over-strong relative to the outside base rate.

CAPACITY IS NOT THE CONSTRAINT AT $750k; EXECUTION DESIGN AND LIQUIDATION PATH ARE. FIM's break-even fund size for short-term reversal is $9.45bn US / $12.75bn global; the strategy family stops working somewhere between $10m and $1bn depending on tier and execution. At $750k the book is ~4 orders of magnitude below the wall. Therefore: (i) do not let capacity arguments constrain a size increase in the liquid tier; (ii) DO let them constrain the overflow tier, where the per-name ADV constraint binds at roughly current size; (iii) the real ceilings on a size increase are the exposure-fee/liquidation path and the broker's discretion to raise house margin overnight, both of which are step functions rather than smooth costs.

A CONCRETE HEADROOM MONITOR IS MISSING FROM THE BOOK. Nothing in the repo tracks gross-to-NAV, blended margin rate, or distance to the exposure fee. Given that the book already peaked at ~1.0x NAV in a single strategy with the dial at 89.5, and that a size increase is on the table, the sizing plan should ship with three daily numbers alongside the fragility dial: gross/NAV, blended TIMS rate (stock 15% / index 8% / 3x 45% or 90%), and implied loss under a -30% one-day equity scenario as a fraction of NAV. Those are computable from the existing /exec-book snapshot and betas.json that the hedge panel already reads.
contested_points: FIM vs Novy-Marx-Velikov on whether short-term reversal is investable at all. FIM (live $1.7tn of executions) put STR's realized cost at 6.75%/yr against a break-even of 8.27%/yr - i.e. VIABLE at their ~$1.5bn implied scale, with a break-even fund size of $9.45bn. Novy-Marx & Velikov (TAQ effective spreads) put STR at gross 0.37%/mo against 1.65%/mo of cost, i.e. net -1.28%/mo, DEAD at any scale. The gap is a cost-measurement dispute: FIM measure what a sophisticated trader actually paid (patient, liquidity-taking-averse, ~12-20 bps), NMV apply full effective spreads to every rebalance. For a book whose entries are passive limits, FIM's measurement is the more relevant one - but it is also the self-reported cost of the firm selling the conclusion, so treat the truth as between them and closer to FIM for limit-entry strategies, closer to NMV for market-order strategies.

Almgren's 3/5 exponent vs the 1/2 square-root law. Almgren et al. (2005) explicitly reject the square root for temporary impact in favor of a 3/5 power law; Toth/Bouchaud/Bershova-Rakhlin and a decade of metaorder studies find 0.5 (0.4-0.7 range, 0.6 for large-tick names). The difference matters little in the 0.25-2% ADV band this book trades (both give 2-25 bps) and matters a lot above 10% ADV, where the 3/5 law is more pessimistic. Use 0.5 for planning and 0.6 as the stress case.

IBKR's concentration trigger is undisclosed. The 30% concentration minimum is published, the threshold that classifies a position as 'a large single concentration' is not. Third-party summaries cite a single name exceeding ~50% of the portfolio; IBKR's own text only says PM 'must assess proportionately larger margin for accounts with positions which represent a concentration in a relatively small number of stocks'. Any gross-ceiling plan should be stress-tested at BOTH 15% and 30% per-name rates, because the transition point cannot be predicted from published rules and the OLV stacking pattern (10 names, 84% of NAV) is squarely in the ambiguous zone.

Whether the 'higher of rules-based and portfolio margin' rule applies to US-resident PM accounts. That sentence appears on IBKR's non-US-resident stock margin page. If it applies, short 3x ETF legs are margined at 90% of notional rather than the 45% TIMS stress, and the blended ceiling for a book with meaningful 3x exposure roughly halves. This is directly checkable in the live account's margin report and should be verified before any size increase rather than assumed either way.

Direction of volatility-conditioned sizing. Nagel (2012) says the liquidity-provision premium and the conditional Sharpe of reversal strategies rise sharply with VIX, implying size UP in stress. The repo's own PIT re-estimation says the FAMILY4 dip-buys degrade at dial >= 50 (hi -0.10R vs lo +0.63R, clustered t -1.96, negative in 6 of 9 years) implying size DOWN. Both can be true: the repo's dial is a composite of fragility signals, not VIX, and the repo's entries are selective rather than the full cross-sectional reversal book Nagel studies. But an orchestrator writing a sizing plan should not treat 'cut size when volatility is high' as an outside-evidence-supported prior - it is not; the outside prior is the opposite, and the repo's finding is a book-specific override.

Whether the -30% exposure-fee scenario is the right binding constraint. IBKR states the fee targets accounts adversely affected by a 1-day 30% equity-market drop and names concentrated single positions as the driver, but the actual formula is proprietary, changes without notice, and averages losses across an undisclosed scenario set. The practical answer is empirical: query the Exposure Fee Calculation Report in Client Portal at current size, then at 2x and 3x hypothetical gross via the Risk Navigator custom-scenario feature, before committing to a gross ceiling on paper.

Nagel's Sharpe 8.44 is not achievable and he says so. The raw number is gross of all costs, uses transaction prices (which embed the bid-ask capture), and the paper attributes the non-arbitrage to fixed costs of high-speed market access rather than to risk. Do not let the 8.44 anchor any expectation for this book; the relevant figure from that paper is the 0.30 vs 0.18 %/day spread (the liquidity-provision component) and the VIX conditioning, not the level.
